papers.full_text: Recent outbreaks with viruses such as Bundibugyo virus and Andes virus are a reminder that another pandemic can happen at any time. This Comment summarizes where we stand with pandemic preparedness from a vaccine perspective. During the COVID-19 pandemic, we witnessed vaccine development at its finest. Vaccines against the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 were developed at record speed and were made available within approximately 1 year after the outbreak started1. This swift development of vaccines was facilitated by new technologies such as the mRNA vaccine platform2 but also by a wealth of existing knowledge because of many years of virology, vaccinology and structural biology research. Much has happened since the COVID-19 pandemic. Technology has evolved, new insights into mechanisms of protection and basic immunology have been gained and regulatory and policy views have changed (Fig. 1), especially in the USA. Where does this leave us with vaccine preparedness for emerging pathogens? Mucosal immunity matters A clear lesson learned from the COVID-19 pandemic was that intramuscular vaccination can only imperfectly protect from infection with respiratory viruses per se and from onward transmission1. Vaccines that are administered via mucosal surfaces may be a better option to induce immunity in the upper respiratory tract to protect from infection with respiratory viruses. This was clearly identified as a gap, and funding agencies, including the US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) and Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority (BARDA), set out to support the development of mucosal vaccine approaches for COVID-19 (ref. 3). Unfortunately, funding for many of these vaccines was terminated or redirected to other projects owing to the policy decision that COVID-19 is no longer a priority. However, having infection- and transmission-blocking vaccines early in an outbreak with a respiratory virus would notably increase the effect of vaccines. Although several intranasal vaccines for COVID-19 are either still in development or already licensed outside the USA and Europe4,5, there is a large gap in terms of vaccine preparedness when it comes to mucosal vaccination routes. Having mucosal vaccines with clear immunological (and potentially mucosal) correlates of protection and established vaccine efficacy and safety on the market would increase confidence in these vaccine platforms and would likely enable early deployment during an outbreak or a pandemic. Broadly protective or strain-specific vaccines Studies of influenza virus and HIV-1 have shown that RNA viruses can evolve quickly. This was also observed with SARS-CoV-2. With the emergence of the Omicron variants, vaccines had to be updated to stay effective. However, updating vaccines to respond to emerging variants means always being one step behind the virus. This is a scenario with which we are very familiar from influenza virus vaccines. Owing to the antigenic variability of RNA viruses, the development of broadly protective vaccines has been the focus in the HIV-1 and influenza fields for many years but also became an important topic for SARS-CoV-2. The concept of broadly protective vaccines goes further than the idea of covering evolving virus variants. The idea has expanded to develop vaccines that potentially can protect from whole virus families, which would considerably increase pandemic preparedness. Although funding for such vaccines has been made available (for example, via the NIAID Collaborative Influenza Vaccine Innovation Centers program, the BARDA funding initiatives and the European Health and Digital Executive Agency), they have not progressed far enough to be used in case of an emergency. Further investment is urgently needed to advance these candidates and concepts through clinical development and realize their potential as tools to combat evolving viral threats and future pandemics. In addition, the regulatory pathway to get such vaccines licensed remains unclear. Vaccines need to be tested in phase 3 efficacy trials to show how well they protect against disease. To demonstrate that a vaccine is broadly protective, multi-year trials to show efficacy in seasons with antigenic changes are likely needed, and such trials may be prohibitively expensive. Furthermore, demonstrating efficacy against pathogens that are not yet circulating in humans is impossible, making it difficult to claim universal protection against future pathogens with pandemic potential. For pandemic preparedness, strain-matched vaccines that can be generated rapidly after the emergence of a new virus currently seems to be favored over the development of broadly protective vaccines (for example, https://cepi.net/100-days). Although this is of course also a good approach, it would be better to have vaccines ready before a new outbreak even starts and not months later, which is something that a broadly protective or universal vaccine could deliver. Pandemic influenza breakthroughs The recent pan-zootic with highly pathogenic H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b influenza virus and its spillover into many mammalian species has raised concerns about the potential of this virus to cause a pandemic6. Fortunately, recent developments have enhanced pandemic influenza vaccine preparedness. For influenza vaccines, a correlate of protection accepted by regulators exists — the hemagglutination inhibition titer — although several other validated correlates of protection have also been established by academic researchers7. If a vaccine manufacturer has a licensed seasonal influenza virus vaccine on the market, the same technology can be used to manufacture a vaccine for an emerging pandemic influenza virus strain and get it to the market based on this correlate, instead of performing time-consuming phase 3 field efficacy trials first. Although effectiveness must be confirmed later, this step saves a lot of time during an outbreak. So far, this pathway has been open to manufacturers who are producing influenza vaccines using traditional technologies, such as split-inactivated vaccines. To update these vaccines to a new pandemic strain can be time-consuming. This process can be faster using the mRNA platform, but until recently, no mRNA-based seasonal influenza vaccines were available, meaning that this quick strain-change pathway was not open to the mRNA technology. The recent licensure of an mRNA-based seasonal influenza vaccine from Moderna (mFLUSIVA in the USA; mCOMBRIAX in the European Union) changed this8. Although the benefits of an mRNA-based seasonal influenza vaccine compared with conventional vaccines remain debated, the advantage in terms of speed in case of a pandemic is a game changer. Using the mechanism of a strain change from seasonal strains to a pandemic strain in combination with the mRNA technology may make it possible to have a matched pandemic influenza vaccine ready for use in the population within 3 months. The Bundibugyo virus outbreak as a test In May 2026, an outbreak with Bundibugyo virus was reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)9. This outbreak is still ongoing, case numbers are growing and it has now become the second largest outbreak of Ebola disease in recorded history. Although vaccines against another virus species, Ebola virus (formerly known as Zaire ebolavirus), are licensed and available, strain-matched vaccines for Bundibugyo virus had not been clinically developed10. This crisis in the DRC serves as test for post-COVID-19 pandemic vaccine preparedness. So far, two vaccines have moved into clinical evaluation. The first phase 1 trial, based on an adenovirus vector (ChAdOx1-BDBV-GP), began in July in the UK11. A second trial, with an mRNA vaccine, was initiated in August in Canada (mRNA-1469, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07737717). How long it takes to move these vaccines forward in the clinical pipeline, whether they are successful, and if they are fast enough to be used in the current outbreak remain to be determined. It is, however, noteworthy that these two vaccines are based on the same technologies that delivered the first COVID-19 vaccines. The value of basic research for vaccine preparedness Another aspect that needs to be mentioned is basic research that is being conducted to better understand emerging viruses that have so far gained little interest, especially viruses belonging to the Bunyaviricetes. This class includes viruses such as severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV), Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHVF), Toscana virus (TOSV), Heartland virus, Shamonda virus, Yezo virus12 and Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV)13, as well as hantaviruses such as Andes virus14. Some of these viruses are already human-to-human transmissible and have caused concerning outbreaks, such as the Andes virus outbreak in May on the cruise ship MV Hondius15. The spike proteins of these viruses were not well understood, making vaccine design complicated. Recent advances in understanding the molecular biology, structural biology and antigenicity of these viruses, partially funded by the excellent NIAID Research and Development of Vaccines and Monoclonal Antibodies for Pandemic Preparedness (ReVAMPP) program, have started to change that. Using new technologies and insights, vaccines against these challenging targets can now potentially also be developed quickly if needed, highlighting the need for and value of basic research. Conclusions The obvious question is, are we now, after the COVID-19 pandemic, better prepared for coming epidemics and pandemics in respect to vaccines? The answer is not a simple yes or no. Technology has advanced, our understanding of virus biology has markedly increased and COVID-19 has shown us that vaccines can be developed quickly if needed and if an effort is made by all stakeholders. However, there is much still to learn; from basic research and clinical testing to manufacturing and regulatory policies. Importantly, funding policies and regulatory policies are changing in parts of the world, partially influenced by the anti-vaccine movement that now has advocates within governments. It is unclear what the long-term effect of these changes is on vaccine development and pandemic preparedness. References - Krammer, F. Semin. papers.title_original: Vaccine preparedness for the next emerging infectious disease crisis

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the need for improved vaccine preparedness against emerging infectious diseases, highlighting the importance of learning from the rapid development of vaccines for SARS-CoV-2.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a commentary analyzing vaccine preparedness strategies, focusing on the lessons learned from the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic and the challenges in developing vaccines for emerging pathogens such as Bundibugyo virus.
analysis.methods: The methods involve a review of existing vaccine technologies, regulatory pathways, and funding initiatives, with an emphasis on mucosal immunity and the development of broadly protective vaccines.
analysis.main_results: The Bundibugyo virus outbreak in May 2026 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo served as a test for post-COVID-19 pandemic vaccine preparedness, and the study notes that the benefits of mRNA-based seasonal influenza vaccines compared to conventional ones remain debated, though their speed in case of a pandemic is a significant advantage.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that while strain-matched vaccines are currently favored for pandemic preparedness, the development of broadly protective vaccines could significantly enhance readiness for future viral threats.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the importance of investing in vaccine platforms that can be rapidly deployed and the need for broader research into emerging viruses to improve future pandemic responses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is based on a commentary and does not include direct experimental results, which limits its strength. However, the analysis is grounded in current vaccine development trends and policy decisions.

analysis.summary_en: This commentary discusses the importance of vaccine preparedness for emerging infectious diseases, emphasizing the lessons from the rapid development of SARS-CoV-2 vaccines. It highlights the potential of mucosal vaccines and the challenges in creating broadly protective ones due to antigenic variability. The study notes that the Bundibugyo virus outbreak in May 2026 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo serves as a test for post-COVID-19 pandemic readiness. While strain-matched vaccines are currently favored, the authors suggest that broadly protective vaccines could enhance preparedness for future viral threats. The analysis underscores the need for further investment in vaccine development and basic research, particularly for viruses with pandemic potential. However, the commentary lacks direct experimental results, which limits its evidence strength.

analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是一篇分析 疫苗 准备策略的评论,重点关注从 SARS-CoV-2 大流行中汲取的经验教训以及针对本迪布焦病毒等新兴病原体开发 疫苗 的挑战。
analysis_zh.methods: 这些方法涉及对现有 疫苗 技术、监管途径和资助计划的审查,重点是粘膜免疫和广泛保护性 疫苗 的开发。

analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,虽然毒株匹配的 疫苗 目前在大流行防范方面受到青睐,但广泛保护的 疫苗 的开发可以显着增强对未来病毒威胁的准备。

papers.full_text: Abstract Objectives Although risk communication is essential to infectious disease crisis response, in the Republic of Korea, infectious disease crisis management exercises have mainly focused on field response procedures, with few exercises specifically addressing risk communication. This paper describes the implementation of a risk communication tabletop exercise developed and conducted by the Office of the Spokesperson at the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency and presents the identified improvement tasks and implications. Methods The World Health Organization’s Simulation Exercise Manual (2017) was used to develop a discussion-based tabletop exercise using Ebola virus disease and avian influenza scenarios. The exercise aimed to evaluate risk communication procedures at each crisis alert level, clarify team roles and external cooperation systems, and identify improvement areas. The exercise simulated escalating crisis alert levels through a spokesperson-led communication review meeting, followed by post-exercise discussion. Results Briefing procedures, centralized press inquiry channels, misinformation and disinformation monitoring procedures, and communication channels for external cooperation operated smoothly during the exercise. In areas where standards and roles had not been sufficiently specified, ad hoc responses were observed. The exercise identified areas for improvement in emergency communication content, public campaigns, press communication, implementation of external cooperation, and personnel and organizational operations. Conclusions Repeated peacetime exercises can strengthen risk communication. This case may provide a basis for developing evaluation frameworks, expanding participation, and promoting the standardization and institutionalization of risk communication exercises. Key words: Health communication, Risk communication, Communicable diseases, Disaster planning, Simulation training Key messages 1 What is known previously? Although essential to infectious disease crisis response, risk communication has received limited attention in Korean exercises, which have mainly focused on field response procedures. 2 What new information is presented? The Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency Office of the Spokesperson conducted its first tabletop exercise dedicated to risk communication. Briefing, press inquiry, monitoring of misinformation and disinformation, and external cooperation procedures ran smoothly. The exercise identified areas for improvement in emergency content, public campaigns, press communication, external cooperation implementation, and personnel and organizational operations. 3 What are implications? Repeated exercises, objective evaluation indicators, broader participation, and diverse scenarios are needed to strengthen and institutionalize risk communication training. Introduction In an infectious disease crisis, risk communication is a core response function alongside disease control measures. Systematic risk communication is necessary to earn public trust, induce voluntary compliance with prevention guidelines during the introduction and spread of novel infectious diseases, and respond to misinformation and disinformation. Risk communication has evolved beyond simple information delivery into a specialized field that plans and coordinates messages and communication channels according to the crisis stage, public risk perception, and information needs [1,2]. The World Health Organization (WHO) also presents risk communication as a core pillar of infectious disease response and addresses it as a major indicator in the evaluation of International Health Regulations implementation [3,4]. In the Republic of Korea as well, awareness of the importance of risk communication has increased through the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), but a training system to check this during routine times has not been sufficiently established. The Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency (KDCA) has conducted infectious disease crisis management response exercises for local governments and related organizations since 2010 [5]. However, there were limitations in checking functions unique to risk communication, such as briefings, media relations, public communication, and management of misinformation and disinformation, because these were centered on practical disease control procedures including case identification, reporting, epidemiological investigation, and contact management. Accordingly, for the first time, the Spokesperson’s Office of the KDCA designed and conducted its own tabletop exercise specialized for risk communication. This paper aims to introduce the design and execution process of the exercise, and share the identified improvement tasks and implications. Main Body 1. Design and Execution of the Risk Communication Tabletop Exercise The Spokesperson’s Office selected a discussion-based tabletop exercise suitable for checking plans and procedures, referring to the WHO’s Simulation Exercise Manual (2017) [6]. According to the manual, a problem statement, injects providing detailed situational updates, and a post-exercise debriefing were applied; reflecting the characteristics of the Spokesperson’s Office’s internal exercise, a communication review meeting format chaired by the spokesperson and a red team that raises questions and checks vulnerabilities in the response were added. The exercise objectives were established with three goals: checking whether response procedures for each crisis alert level are operational, confirming the division of roles among teams and external collaboration systems including experts and digital platforms, and deriving improvement tasks. The exercise planning manager selected Ebola virus disease and human infection with avian influenza, which have different transmission patterns, and a risk communication practitioner drafted scenarios based on the transmission characteristics and spread situations of the infectious diseases. The drafted scenarios were internally reviewed by three managers in the Spokesperson’s Office for alignment with the exercise objectives. The scenarios were shared 2 weeks prior to the exercise to check the level of preparation and feasibility of existing procedures rather than immediate response capabilities. Each person in charge prepared response materials for their respective assigned duties by referring to manuals related to infectious disease disasters, standard operating procedures for public health risk communication, and initial risk communication response procedures. The exercise was conducted for approximately 3 hours on June 1, 2026, with the participation of 21 staff members from the Spokesperson’s Office. The participants included 1 spokesperson, 7 in media communication, 6 in digital communication, 5 in communication strategy and operational support, and 2 in the red team. There were 10 participants with experience in infectious disease disaster communication tasks such as COVID-19, and 11 without experience. Time was allocated as follows: 10 minutes for exercise orientation, 120 minutes for scenario-based plan reporting and Q&A, and 50 minutes for a comprehensive discussion. The Ebola virus disease scenario assumed a situation in which excessive fear and stigma were likely to occur due to limited transmission and a high case fatality rate after domestic introduction, whereas the scenario for human infection with avian influenza assumed a situation in which human-to-human transmission expanded and community transmission began. The primary task for the former was reducing excessive fear and stigma while communicating accurate transmission routes, whereas for the latter, it was managing uncertainty and inducing voluntary public participation. The exercise proceeded across three situations: preparing for the occurrence of the first confirmed case of Ebola virus disease, a surge in media and online information demand following the initial briefing, and community transmission of human infection with avian influenza (Table 1). Table 1. Problem statements, key injects, and exercise tasks in infectious disease risk communication tabletop exercise. | Problem statement | Inject | Key exercise tasks | Planned duration | |---|---|---|---| | Situation 1. Preparing for the first confirmed case of Ebola virus disease (crisis alert level: Attention) | Initial test result was positive (06:00); confirmatory test results were expected at 13:00 | Five plans were reviewed: initial briefing, a unified press inquiry channel, response to mis- and disinformation, public communication content preparation, and risk communication team organization; 15 anticipated questions to review the plans | 50 min | | Situation 2. Surge in information demand following the initial briefing on Ebola virus disease (crisis alert level: Caution) | Surge in press inquiries; speculative media coverage; spread of mis- and disinformation, and stigmatizing posts | Three plans were presented: public sentiment-based communication strategy, public risk communication, and expert communication advisory group operations; three anticipated questions to review the plans; one unexpected event (response to inaccurate reporting) | 30 min | | Situation 3. Community transmission of avian influenza in humans (crisis alert level: Alert) | 12 cumulative confirmed cases within 2 weeks; community transmission confirmed, with additional cases of unknown origin reported | Two plans were presented: a public sentiment-based communication strategy and a public risk communication plan; five anticipated questions to review the plans; two unexpected scenarios (concerns over mask supply, media reporting of internal information) | 40 min | The facilitator delivered problem statements and injects through verbal explanation, printed situation descriptions, and the main screen in the exercise room. The numbers of reporting items, anticipated questions, and unexpected events are based on items prepared in advance. Before the exercise, 10 reporting items for response plans across the three situations, 23 anticipated questions to review the detailed content of the plans, and 3 unexpected situations requiring additional response were prepared. The anticipated questions were designed to check the specificity and feasibility of risk communication procedures, such as communication with vulnerable groups, identification of information voids, and improvement of message acceptance. The unexpected situations were set as the occurrence of misreporting, unstable mask supply, and the reporting of non-public information. The spokesperson chaired the meeting, whereas the exercise manager concurrently handled exercise facilitation and recording, with no separate observer assigned. Deputy directors in charge of each domain reported the response materials prepared in advance and answered questions. The red team, consisting of two senior deputy directors with risk communication response experience, raised additional questions during the scenario reporting and Q&A process on areas deemed to require supplementation. Questions focused on vulnerabilities in the response, such as consistent messaging, addressing information voids, content production, and personnel operation, while the pre-prepared anticipated questions were flexibly utilized depending on the reported contents. The exercise manager manually recorded the main discussion points and audio-recorded the entire process. In the scenario-based Q&A and comprehensive discussion, matters requiring the specification of standards and roles, as well as newly identified areas for improvement, were discussed. Subsequently, the exercise records, including the transcripts, were reviewed to summarize improvement opinions, which were categorized into five domains: urgent content, public campaigns, media communication, external collaboration, and personnel/organizational operation, and were finalized after review by three managers in the Spokesperson’s Office. 2. Key Response Procedures Examined in the Exercise In the situational response reporting and post-exercise discussion, areas that were already systematized and smoothly implemented were also identified. The briefing room checks, guidance for press corps and foreign media, support for on-site coverage, and support for sign language interpretation and broadcast relay included in the briefing plan were presented as checklists by the person in charge from case confirmation to holding the briefing. A channel for centralizing media inquiries from the press corps through the Spokesperson’s Office was operating, and article modification requests for misreports and the distribution procedures for explanatory materials on media reports also functioned smoothly. A basic communication foundation for external collaboration and for monitoring misinformation and disinformation was also established during normal times. Step-by-step response procedures, progressing from public opinion monitoring to expert connection for factual information verification, factual information dissemination, and review/investigation requests, were prepared. Communication channels through which cooperation could be requested from media associations and portal and social media businesses, as well as regular communication channels with local governments, were also confirmed. Taken together, key risk communication functions such as briefings, media communication, management of mis- and disinformation, and external collaboration had basic procedures and communication foundations in place, and response plans by person in charge were presented relatively specifically in the exercise. 3. Improvement Tasks Derived Through Exercise Representative questions raised in the exercise included “Are contents to be distributed with the initial press release prepared?” (Emergency content), “Is a public campaign emphasizing social solidarity effective at the current stage?” (Public campaign), “Are the timing and scope of information disclosure to be guided to the press corps before the initial briefing determined?” (Media communication), and “Are there targets among influencers or experts who can immediately collaborate in a crisis situation?” (External collaboration). The staffing and organizational operation tasks were derived by discussing additional personnel requirements and job adjustment plans in the comprehensive discussion. Based on this, improvement tasks in five areas were derived (Table 2). Table 2. Issues identified and directions for improvement from the risk communication tabletop exercise. | Category | Key issues | Directions for improvement | |---|---|---| | Emergency public communication content | Need to improve the preparedness of basic content and visual materials | Prepare scenario-specific basic content and visual materials in advance; develop content templates in advance | | Public campaigns | Unclear criteria for determining when to launch campaigns; need to compile and organize previous campaign cases | Establish criteria for determining the timing of campaigns by response phase; organize previous campaign cases by timing and target audience | | Press communication | Unclear timing and scope of information in briefing notices; insufficient communication channels for reporters outside the press corps; information provision focused primarily on outbreak situation and response measures | Establish standards for briefing notices; establish a communication channel for reporters outside the press corps; develop communication procedures reflecting information voids | | External cooperation (specification of cooperation arrangements) | Communication channels are in place, but specific roles and crisis cooperation arrangements have not been established | Designate experts for broadcast appearances and media consultation; identify influencers for cooperation; specify cooperation arrangements with digital platforms | | Personnel and organizational operations | Need to improve the design of standard staffing and role assignments based on crisis level; addressing workload from concurrent crisis response duties and concerns about equitable staff treatment | Establish standard staffing and task assignments by crisis alert level; predefine tasks to be continued, suspended, or expanded during a crisis | First, it was confirmed that basic content in preparation for emergency situations was not sufficiently prepared, which could make rapid distribution of content difficult in the event of a crisis. In particular, as in the early stages of the mpox outbreak in 2022, if provocative images are circulated first, it can lead to excessive risk perception and anxiety. Therefore, it is necessary to prepare basic content by scenario, visual materials, and templates that can be quickly used in advance. Second, the criteria for determining when to deploy public campaigns according to the crisis phase were not sufficiently specific. Accordingly, it is necessary to systematically organize campaign cases implemented in past infectious disease crises, focusing on timing and main contents, and establish criteria for determining the timing of campaign promotion according to crisis situations based on this. Third, although guidance text messages are sent to the press corps before holding a briefing, the appropriate timing of sending and the scope of information to be included in the guidance text were unclear, and communication channels for non-press corps journalists were also insufficient. Accordingly, the need to establish briefing guidance standards and communication channels for non-press corps journalists was raised. In addition, it is necessary to establish a communication procedure that starts from public opinion analysis and leads to briefings to move away from information delivery centered on health authorities and identify information voids and communicate with the public accordingly. analysis.summary_en: This study describes the implementation of a risk communication tabletop exercise by the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, highlighting the need for systematic risk communication during infectious disease crises. The exercise simulated scenarios based on Ebola virus disease and avian influenza, aiming to evaluate procedures, clarify team roles, and identify improvement areas. Key results showed that some communication processes operated smoothly, while others required ad hoc responses. The authors emphasize the importance of structured risk communication to build public trust and ensure compliance with prevention guidelines. The study identifies potential areas for enhancement in emergency communication, public campaigns, and external cooperation. However, the findings are based on a single case and lack quantitative data, limiting the strength of the evidence to moderate.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在评估韩国风险沟通桌面演习的实施情况,并确定需要改进的领域,韩国此类演习主要侧重于现场响应程序,而不是风险沟通本身。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 韩国疾病管理和预防机构发言人办公室进行了基于讨论的桌面演习,通过发言人主导的沟通审查会议模拟危机警报级别的升级。参与者包括发言人1名、媒体传播7名、数字传播6名、传播策略和运营支持5名、红队2名。
elements_zh.methods: 该演习是根据世界卫生组织的模拟演习手册(2017)开发的,涉及基于埃博拉病毒病和禽流感的场景。参与者参考手册、标准操作程序和初始风险沟通应对程序准备应对材料。
elements_zh.main_results: 演习期间,通报程序、新闻集中询问渠道、错误信息和虚假信息监测程序、对外合作沟通渠道运行顺利。然而,标准和角色尚未充分明确的领域则采取了临时应对措施。此次演练确定了应急通信内容、公众宣传、新闻传播、对外合作实施、人员和组织运作等方面的改进领域。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,系统的风险沟通对于赢得公众信任、促使自愿遵守预防指南以及应对错误信息和虚假信息是必要的。该研究提出了在韩国实施专门风险沟通桌面演习的新案例。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果可以为风险沟通活动评估框架的制定提供信息,促进此类做法的标准化和制度化,并通过改进沟通策略加强对传染病危机的准备。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于单个案例,并未提供演习有效性的定量数据。证据是温和的,因为它是基于对桌面练习的描述性分析而不是实证结果。

papers.title: Managing occupational dermatitis during pandemics using virucidal emollient Dermol 500.
papers.abstract: BackgroundWork-related contact dermatitis is a significant problem for healthcare workers. Repeated exposure to water, soap and alcohol-based gels can cause dry skin, irritation and contact dermatitis. Soap substitutes such as Dermol 500 are commonly prescribed to prevent and treat dermatitis. However, hand hygiene recommendations during the COVID-19 pandemic advised against using soap substitutes in clinical settings as their virucidal capacity had not been established. AimsTo investigate whether Dermol 500 lotion exhibits virucidal activity and is a suitable soap substitute for use during viral disease outbreaks. This study aims to inform best practice in occupational medicine and help combat the increased incidence of work-related contact dermatitis in clinical settings. MethodsThe virucidal activity of Dermol 500 lotion and its antimicrobial constituents benzalkonium chloride (BAK) and chlorhexidine dihydrochloride (CD) was assessed against influenza A virus (IAV), SARS-CoV-2 and pseudotyped viruses expressing glycoproteins from 2026 outbreak strains of Ebolavirus and Hantavirus. Viruses or pseudoviruses were incubated with treatment prior to quenching serial dilution and infectivity measurement by plaque assay, tissue culture infectious dose 50 (TCID50) or bioluminescent reporter activity. ResultsDermol 500 exhibits comparable virucidal activity to alcohol-based hand sanitisers against IAV and SARS-CoV-2. Furthermore, the Dermol 500 components BAK and CD exhibit independent and synergistic virucidal activity against IAV, SARS-CoV-2 and pseudoviruses. ConclusionsThe virucidal activity of Dermol 500 lotion and its active antimicrobials BAK and CD indicates its suitability as a soap substitute to treat and prevent contact dermatitis in front line workers during viral disease outbreaks. Teaser textOccupational dermatitis soared during the COVID-19 pandemic, but the standard treatment - the antimicrobial emollient and soap substitute Dermol 500 - was not recommended as its antiviral activity was unknown. Here, we address this evidence gap: Dermol 500 lotion is an effective virucide, and its constituents benzalkonium chloride (BAK) and chlorhexidine dihydrochloride (CD) effectively neutralise SARS-CoV-2, influenza A virus and pseudotyped 2026 strains of Ebolavirus and Hantavirus at concentrations 10-fold lower than the active formulation.

MethodsThe virucidal activity of Dermol 500 lotion and its antimicrobial constituents benzalkonium chloride (BAK) and chlorhexidine dihydrochloride (CD) was assessed against influenza A virus (IAV), SARS-CoV-2 and pseudotyped viruses expressing glycoproteins from 2026 outbreak strains of Ebolavirus and Hantavirus. ConclusionsThe virucidal activity of Dermol 500 lotion and its active antimicrobials BAK and CD indicates its suitability as a soap substitute to treat and prevent contact dermatitis in front line workers during viral disease outbreaks. papers.abstract_zh: 背景与工作相关的接触性皮炎是医护人员面临的一个重大问题。反复接触水、肥皂和酒精凝胶会导致皮肤干燥、刺激和接触性皮炎。Dermol 500 等肥皂替代品通常用于预防和治疗皮炎。然而,COVID-19 大流行期间的手部卫生建议建议不要在临床环境中使用肥皂替代品,因为其杀病毒能力尚未确定。目的研究 Dermol 500 洗剂是否具有杀病毒活性,是否适合在病毒性疾病 暴发 期间使用肥皂替代品。本研究旨在为职业医学的最佳实践提供信息,并帮助对抗临床环境中与工作相关的接触性皮炎的增加。方法评估了 Dermol 500 洗剂及其抗菌成分苯扎氯铵 (BAK) 和二盐酸氯己定 (CD) 对甲型流感病毒 (IAV)、SARS-CoV-2 以及表达埃博拉病毒和汉坦病毒 2026 暴发 株糖蛋白的假型病毒的杀病毒活性。将病毒或假病毒与 治疗 一起孵育,然后通过噬菌斑测定、组织培养感染剂量 50 (TCID50) 或生物发光报告活性进行淬灭连续稀释和感染性测量。结果 Dermol 500 对 IAV 和 SARS-CoV-2 表现出与酒精类洗手液相当的杀病毒活性。此外,Dermol 500 成分 BAK 和 CD 对 IAV、SARS-CoV-2 和假病毒表现出独立和协同的杀病毒活性。结论 Dermol 500 洗剂及其活性抗菌剂 BAK 和 CD 的杀病毒活性表明其适合作为肥皂替代品来治疗和预防病毒性疾病 暴发 期间一线工作人员的接触性皮炎。预告片文字在 COVID-19 大流行期间,职业性皮炎激增,但标准 治疗(抗菌润肤剂和肥皂替代品 Dermol 500)并未得到推荐,因为其 抗病毒药物 活性未知。在此,我们解决了这一证据差距:Dermol 500 洗剂是一种有效的杀病毒剂,其成分苯扎氯铵 (BAK) 和二盐酸氯己定 (CD) 可以有效中和 SARS-CoV-2、甲型流感病毒以及埃博拉病毒和汉坦病毒的假型 2026 株,浓度比活性制剂低 10 倍。

Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA DR Congo + 6 more Multi-country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak Situation Report No. 27 (9 - 15 November 2026) Format Situation Report Source IOM Posted 20 Nov 2026 Originally published 20 Nov 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Report (PDF | 4.09 MB) IOM REGIONAL RESPONSE AT A GLANCE During the reporting period (9–15 November 2026), IOM supported 3,729,851 traveller screenings, bringing the cumulative total to 79,831,882 screenings since the start of the outbreak. Thirty-nine alerts were identified through IOM-supported surveillance – 28 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), 1 in Uganda and 10 in the Central African Republic (CAR) – bringing the cumulative total to 1,034 alerts. At IOM-supported points of entry (PoEs) and points of control (PoCs) in DRC, five deceased persons were intercepted and referred for sample collection and safe and dignified burial, bringing the cumulative total to 271. One confirmed Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease (BVD) case was reported in a displacement site, bringing the cumulative number of confirmed cases detected through IOM-supported surveillance to 73. IOM reached 3,073,123 people through risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) during the reporting period, bringing the cumulative reach to 68,933,505 people since the start of the outbreak. The announcement highlights efforts to strengthen health systems and respond to potential outbreaks. However, the evidence does not mention any confirmed cases, deaths, or specific risk levels associated with the Bundibugyo virus in South Sudan. The focus is on readiness and prevention measures rather than an active outbreak. transformation WHO Africa / Countries / South Sudan / South Sudan strengthens readiness for Bundibugyo virus disease South Sudan strengthens readiness for Bundibugyo virus disease 20 November 2026 | Feature Story | Reading time: 4 min South Sudan strengthens readiness for Bundibugyo virus disease More pictures More images Juba—South Sudan has taken steps to improve its ability to detect and respond to a potential Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak, following the declaration of the outbreak in neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo on 15 May 2026. The country conducted four successive national readiness self-assessment in 2026, using a WHO tool that reviews the quality of core functional areas of an emergency response. The assessment showed that the country’s readiness score increased from 29% in May 2026 to 72.5% in October 2026. It also identified gaps in preparedness and informed efforts to improve surveillance, screening, isolation and referral. Furthermore, the country conducted a sub-national risk assessment that identified 15 high-risk counties to help authorities identify priority areas for targeted preparedness activities and resource allocation. Prioritization was based on proximity to affected areas in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, known population movements, location of formal and informal border crossings, surveillance gaps and local vulnerabilities. The WHO African Region's artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled Preparedness Data Exchange (PDX), which integrates preparedness and risk data to inform early, evidence-based decisions across the region, supported the analysis. In June 2026, 50 national public health institute workers, supported by 20 national and international partner agencies, participated in scenario-based table-top simulation exercise aimed at testing the completeness and comprehensiveness of the country’s BVD preparedness and readiness plan. Between July and September, health authorities conducted drills at newly established isolation facilities and the National Public Health Laboratories. A specific infection prevention and control drill was organised at the national level to improve the skills of national rapid response team members and their implementing partners in use of personal protective equipment, chlorine preparation and use and disinfection of potentially infectious materials. From 19 to 24 October 2026, the country conducted a full-scale simulation exercise to test how its emergency response systems would function during a potential BVD outbreak. The exercise brought together 93 participants from Ministry of Health, government institutions, WHO, United Nations agencies and implementing partners. The week-long exercise allowed teams to assess functional status of the response areas, the hand-offs between these areas, how they share information, coordinated their actions and carry out their responsibilities. “The simulation exercise allowed South Sudan to identify strengths and best practices, close gaps and define priorities to improve national capabilities to safely identify and isolate suspected BVD cases, protect the lives and health of our prized health workers and indeed the people of South Sudan,” said Honourable Dak Duop Bichiok, Caretaker National Minister of Health of South Sudan. With support from WHO, the Ministry of Health activated its Public Health Emergency Operations Centre (PHEOC) to coordinate preparedness activities and bring together response teams and partners. The PHEOC coordinates and monitors BVD preparedness and readiness plan implementation. It also functions as an accountability centre, where roles and responsibilities are assigned to the many team members needed for BVD readiness. “Systems were activated, with teams and resources deployed to high-risk areas to strengthen coordination, early detection, infection prevention and control, safe and dignified burial, case management and risk communication and community engagement,” said Dr Ader Macar Aciek, Acting Executive Director, National Public Health Institute in South Sudan. “The recently concluded full scale simulation exercise tested the country’s capabilities for Ebola outbreak containment before we are contained by the virus itself.” The simulation exercise showed that South Sudan can detect BVD in all simulated sites, including one of the 26 priority points of entry that connect it with neighbouring countries with BVD cases. “Preparedness cannot wait until a case is detected. WHO is working with South Sudan and partners to identify gaps, strengthen response capacities and ensure that teams are ready to act quickly,” said Dr Moses Ongom, Officer-in-Charge at WHO South Sudan. “With the outbreak ongoing in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, maintaining readiness across the region is essential to detecting cases early and preventing further spread of Ebola.” Share Related News See all → Emergency 15 November 2026 | News Release Six months on, accessing hard-to-reach communities key to halting Ebola outbreak 11 November 2026 | News Release Kenya’s last Ebola patient goes home as 42-day countdown begins Emergency 11 November 2026 | News Release Ghana and partners review progress in pandemic fund-supported preparedness efforts Emergency 9 November 2026 | News Release Cabo Verde hosts emergency response training of trainers for African Portuguese-speaking countries

WHO is working with South Sudan and partners to identify gaps, strengthen response capacities and ensure that teams are ready to act quickly,” said Dr Moses Ongom, Officer-in-Charge at WHO South Sudan. “With the outbreak ongoing in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, maintaining readiness across the region is essential to detecting cases early and preventing further spread of Ebola.” Share Related News See all → Emergency 15 November 2026 | News Release Six months on, accessing hard-to-reach communities key to halting Ebola outbreak 11 November 2026 | News Release Kenya’s last Ebola patient goes home as 42-day countdown begins Emergency 11 November 2026 | News Release Ghana and partners review progress in pandemic fund-supported preparedness efforts Emergency 9 November 2026 | News Release Cabo Verde hosts emergency response training of trainers for African Portuguese-speaking countries

analysis.brief_en: South Sudan has taken steps to enhance its readiness for a potential Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak, following the declaration of an outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) on 15 May 2026. The country conducted four national readiness self-assessments in 2026, using a WHO tool, which showed an increase in readiness score from 29% in May to 72.5% in October. Additionally, a sub-national risk assessment identified 15 high-risk counties, prioritized based on proximity to affected areas in DRC, population movements, and local vulnerabilities. Between July and September 2026, health authorities conducted drills at newly established isolation facilities and laboratories, and a full-scale simulation exercise from 19 to 24 October tested the country’s emergency response systems. The exercise involved 93 participants from various institutions, including WHO and the Ministry of Health, and highlighted the ability to detect BVD at 26 priority points of entry. The Public Health Emergency Operations Centre (PHEOC) was activated to coordinate preparedness efforts, with support from WHO and partners. These actions aim to improve surveillance, isolation, and response capabilities to prevent the spread of BVD and protect public health.

Studies DONATE Search Menu Why humans get the worst of Ebola virus Humans and bats can both catch Ebola virus, but only humans get sick. Scientists have uncovered a molecular difference that leaves humans uniquely vulnerable to the deadly virus. Madeline McCurry-Schmidt Science Writer November 19, 2026 Share this Article: What does this new study show? People die from Ebola disease when their immune cells churn out overwhelming levels of inflammatory molecules. Scientists at La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) discovered a reason why human cells are especially vulnerable to this kind of cellular dysfunction. They found that Ebola virus captures specific molecules in human cells, which leaves the body prone to dangerous inflammation. Why compare humans and bats? Bats can carry Ebola virus without getting sick. Researchers need to understand this natural virus control in bats and pinpoint what goes wrong in human patients. In the new study, LJI scientists show why bats are not vulnerable to the same kind of harmful inflammation seen in human cases. Ebola virus forms membraneless condensates (yellow) during infection. LA JOLLA, CA—Illnesses from Ebola virus and its relatives have about a 50 percent fatality rate in humans. The current outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has already caused over 10,500 confirmed cases and over 5,130 deaths, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Ebola virus is a devastating pathogen. Like humans, bats can get infected with Ebola virus. So why don’t bats get sick? “Another puzzle,” says lead author LJI Professor, President & CEO Erica Ollmann Saphire, Ph.D., MBA. “is why humans do get so sick. And why the worst cases can have the strongest inflammatory responses. These are strong immune responses, but they’re not working well.” In a new Cell study, La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) researchers, working in collaboration with Princeton University Professors Aartjan te Velthuis, Ph.D., and Clifford Brangwynne, Ph.D., and UC San Diego Professor Gene Yeo, Ph.D., MBA, share a key reason why humans are especially vulnerable to severe Ebola disease. It may come down to viral “nests.” Ebola virus builds protected, bubble-like “nests” inside host cells, technically termed membraneless condensates. The virus harbors its own viral mRNA inside these compartments. What the researchers found, using a technique called spatial transcriptomics, is that Ebola virus also traps human cellular mRNA molecules inside these nests. When Ebola virus traps certain human mRNAs, the human immune system loses its ability to control dangerous inflammation. Fevers spike, organs fail, and Ebola disease turns deadly. These mRNA molecules look different in bat cells, and they don’t end up trapped by Ebola virus. As a result, bats keep Ebola virus infection in check and never show symptoms. Ebola virus builds a ‘nest’ When Ebola virus enters a host cell—be it human or bat—the virus constructs bubble-like structures called viral condensates (also known as viral factories). To produce progeny, the viral material physically condenses and separates from surrounding cellular content, creating a distinct compartment where viral building blocks are enriched. “When birds land in a new place, they make nests where they can raise their babies. You can imagine viral condensates as nests for a virus,” says Jingru Fang, Ph.D., who led this research as a member of the Saphire Lab at LJI. Saphire and Fang continued the work while Fang was a postdoctoral researcher at Princeton University. As Ebola virus constructs its nest, it pulls in nearby molecules from the host cell. These molecules are called cellular mRNAs. How the body is supposed to fight back Your cells can’t do anything without mRNAs. These little strands of molecules carry instructions from your genes (the “m” in mRNA stands for “messenger”). mRNAs shuttle genetic information from your cell nucleus to a structure called a ribosome. Ribosomes are cellular machines that translate the information encoded in mRNA sequences to build proteins. One copy of mRNA can serve as the blueprint for many copies of proteins. In a healthy cell, mRNAs are meant to do their jobs and then degrade. Message sent, time to go. That timely mRNA degradation is critical for our health, especially for a group of mRNAs encoding defense molecules that help us fight infections. Here’s why: Early in viral infection, those cells that are infected can secrete a molecule, called interferon (IFN), to alert nearby cells of an upcoming infection. This “danger” signal then triggers the expression of a panel of defense genes called Interferon Stimulated Genes or ISGs. The mRNAs of these genes can turn the whole cell into a battlefield against viral invasion—sometimes at the expense of shutting down normal cellular functions. “This is a first line of defense that our bodies can mount,” says Fang. “However, as you can imagine, if this aggressive response is kept up too long, it will cause damage to the host.” The same antiviral defense that kills viruses also harms healthy tissues, so cells are only supposed to turn ISG production “on” for short periods of time. Thanks to mRNA degradation, cells can dial back antiviral response production before tissue damage takes over. “The antiviral response is like a weapon, and cells use degradation as a way to deactivate that weapon,” says Fang. This whole system falls apart when mRNAs get stuck in viral condensates. What goes wrong in humans Out-of-control cytokine production is what kills Ebola disease patients. “In patients with fatal cases, there tends to be this abnormal upregulation of a certain panel of genes that direct the innate immune response,” says Fang. The Saphire Lab specializes in structural biology—the molecular architecture of living things. For the new study, they took a close look at these condensates, and the structural differences between human and bat mRNAs trapped within them. The researchers spotted small differences in the way human and bat mRNA molecules are folded inside cells. They found that human mRNA molecules with certain folded features tended to be recruited into viral condensates more often. Importantly, many of the human mRNAs that got pulled into the condensates were the same mRNAs that normally direct the type I interferon (IFN) response, a rapid antiviral defense mechanism conserved in many cell types as part of the innate immunity. Expression of these powerful defense genes can only be induced by IFN, following rapid degradation to minimize damage. Viral condensates shield these mRNAs from degradation. This means the mRNAs don’t degrade properly, cytokine production stays “on,” and inflammation overwhelms the body. “These are potentially harmful kinds of genes,” says Fang. “And now they’re persisting longer than they normally would.” Bat mRNAs looked different. The scientists examined mRNAs from Egyptian fruit bats, a model fruit bat species and known reservoir species for the related Marburg virus (a relative of Ebola virus). Even though the bats expressed similar mRNAs as humans as part of the conserved antiviral defense, the bat defense mRNAs adopt a different folding feature from human mRNAs, and they were not recruited into viral condensates nearly as often. As a result, says Fang, it appears that the bat immune system can control Ebola virus while keeping harmful inflammation at bay. “We don’t know whether this difference can explain everything, but it gives researchers a place to start looking and confirm what we’ve found in additional human or animal samples,” says Fang. Publication details: Additional authors of the study, “RNA folding drives species-dependent host mRNA partitioning in Ebola virus condensates,” include Dylan C. Lam, Clarence K. Mah, Reika Watanabe, Hailey M. Tanner, Troy Comi, Yuan Cai, Cheng-Yi Chen, Aartjan J. W. te Velthuis, Clifford P. Brangwynne, and Gene W. Yeo. This research received additional support from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, the Princeton Biomolecular Condensate Program, the Princeton Center for Complex Materials, the U.S. National Science Foundation Materials Research Science and Engineering Centers (NSF DMR-2011750), the St. Jude Collaborative on Membraneless Organelles, the AFOSR Multidisciplinary Research Program of the University Research Initiative (FA9550-20-1-0241), the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative Exploratory Cell Network, the National Institutes of Health (grant DP2 AI17547401), and the UC San Diego Sanford Stem Cell Institute. Fang was also supported by The Tullie and Rickey Families SPARK Awards for Innovations in Immunology, through the generosity of LJI Board Director Sandor Shapery and Rebecca Shapery, and a 2025 Omenn Darling Postdoctoral Fellowship through Princeton Bioengineering Institute. About La Jolla Institute La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) was founded in 1988 as an independent, nonprofit research organization. LJI is based in San Diego, CA, and is home to world-class scientists solely focused on immunology. LJI scientists are harnessing the power of the immune system to defeat cancer, autoimmune, infectious, and neurodegenerative diseases. Our breakthroughs in immunology make life without disease possible. Visit lji.org for more information. Studies DONATE Search Menu Why humans get the worst of Ebola virus Humans and bats can both catch Ebola virus, but only humans get sick. Scientists have uncovered a molecular difference that leaves humans uniquely vulnerable to the deadly virus. Madeline McCurry-Schmidt Science Writer November 19, 2026 Share this Article: What does this new study show? People die from Ebola disease when their immune cells churn out overwhelming levels of inflammatory molecules. Scientists at La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) discovered a reason why human cells are especially vulnerable to this kind of cellular dysfunction. They found that Ebola virus captures specific molecules in human cells, which leaves the body prone to dangerous inflammation. Why compare humans and bats? Bats can carry Ebola virus without getting sick. Researchers need to understand this natural virus control in bats and pinpoint what goes wrong in human patients. In the new study, LJI scientists show why bats are not vulnerable to the same kind of harmful inflammation seen in human cases. Ebola virus forms membraneless condensates (yellow) during infection. LA JOLLA, CA—Illnesses from Ebola virus and its relatives have about a 50 percent fatality rate in humans. The current outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has already caused over 10,500 confirmed cases and over 5,130 deaths, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Ebola virus is a devastating pathogen. Like humans, bats can get infected with Ebola virus. So why don’t bats get sick? “Another puzzle,” says lead author LJI Professor, President & CEO Erica Ollmann Saphire, Ph.D., MBA. “is why humans do get so sick. And why the worst cases can have the strongest inflammatory responses. These are strong immune responses, but they’re not working well.” In a new Cell study, La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) researchers, working in collaboration with Princeton University Professors Aartjan te Velthuis, Ph.D., and Clifford Brangwynne, Ph.D., and UC San Diego Professor Gene Yeo, Ph.D., MBA, share a key reason why humans are especially vulnerable to severe Ebola disease. It may come down to viral “nests.” Ebola virus builds protected, bubble-like “nests” inside host cells, technically termed membraneless condensates. The virus harbors its own viral mRNA inside these compartments. What the researchers found, using a technique called spatial transcriptomics, is that Ebola virus also traps human cellular mRNA molecules inside these nests. When Ebola virus traps certain human mRNAs, the human immune system loses its ability to control dangerous inflammation. Fevers spike, organs fail, and Ebola disease turns deadly. These mRNA molecules look different in bat cells, and they don’t end up trapped by Ebola virus. As a result, bats keep Ebola virus infection in check and never show symptoms. Ebola virus builds a ‘nest’ When Ebola virus enters a host cell—be it human or bat—the virus constructs bubble-like structures called viral condensates (also known as viral factories). To produce progeny, the viral material physically condenses and separates from surrounding cellular content, creating a distinct compartment where viral building blocks are enriched. “When birds land in a new place, they make nests where they can raise their babies. You can imagine viral condensates as nests for a virus,” says Jingru Fang, Ph.D., who led this research as a member of the Saphire Lab at LJI. Saphire and Fang continued the work while Fang was a postdoctoral researcher at Princeton University. As Ebola virus constructs its nest, it pulls in nearby molecules from the host cell. These molecules are called cellular mRNAs. How the body is supposed to fight back Your cells can’t do anything without mRNAs. These little strands of molecules carry instructions from your genes (the “m” in mRNA stands for “messenger”). mRNAs shuttle genetic information from your cell nucleus to a structure called a ribosome. Ribosomes are cellular machines that translate the information encoded in mRNA sequences to build proteins. One copy of mRNA can serve as the blueprint for many copies of proteins. In a healthy cell, mRNAs are meant to do their jobs and then degrade. Message sent, time to go. That timely mRNA degradation is critical for our health, especially for a group of mRNAs encoding defense molecules that help us fight infections. Here’s why: Early in viral infection, those cells that are infected can secrete a molecule, called interferon (IFN), to alert nearby cells of an upcoming infection. This “danger” signal then triggers the expression of a panel of defense genes called Interferon Stimulated Genes or ISGs. The mRNAs of these genes can turn the whole cell into a battlefield against viral invasion—sometimes at the expense of shutting down normal cellular functions. “This is a first line of defense that our bodies can mount,” says Fang. “However, as you can imagine, if this aggressive response is kept up too long, it will cause damage to the host.” The same antiviral defense that kills viruses also harms healthy tissues, so cells are only supposed to turn ISG production “on” for short periods of time. Thanks to mRNA degradation, cells can dial back antiviral response production before tissue damage takes over. “The antiviral response is like a weapon, and cells use degradation as a way to deactivate that weapon,” says Fang. This whole system falls apart when mRNAs get stuck in viral condensates. What goes wrong in humans Out-of-control cytokine production is what kills Ebola disease patients. “In patients with fatal cases, there tends to be this abnormal upregulation of a certain panel of genes that direct the innate immune response,” says Fang. The Saphire Lab specializes in structural biology—the molecular architecture of living things. For the new study, they took a close look at these condensates, and the structural differences between human and bat mRNAs trapped within them. The researchers spotted small differences in the way human and bat mRNA molecules are folded inside cells. They found that human mRNA molecules with certain folded features tended to be recruited into viral condensates more often. Importantly, many of the human mRNAs that got pulled into the condensates were the same mRNAs that normally direct the type I interferon (IFN) response, a rapid antiviral defense mechanism conserved in many cell types as part of the innate immunity. Expression of these powerful defense genes can only be induced by IFN, following rapid degradation to minimize damage. Viral condensates shield these mRNAs from degradation. This means the mRNAs don’t degrade properly, cytokine production stays “on,” and inflammation overwhelms the body. “These are potentially harmful kinds of genes,” says Fang. “And now they’re persisting longer than they normally would.” Bat mRNAs looked different. The scientists examined mRNAs from Egyptian fruit bats, a model fruit bat species and known reservoir species for the related Marburg virus (a relative of Ebola virus). Even though the bats expressed similar mRNAs as humans as part of the conserved antiviral defense, the bat defense mRNAs adopt a different folding feature from human mRNAs, and they were not recruited into viral condensates nearly as often. As a result, says Fang, it appears that the bat immune system can control Ebola virus while keeping harmful inflammation at bay. “We don’t know whether this difference can explain everything, but it gives researchers a place to start looking and confirm what we’ve found in additional human or animal samples,” says Fang. Publication details: Additional authors of the study, “RNA folding drives species-dependent host mRNA partitioning in Ebola virus condensates,” include Dylan C. Lam, Clarence K. Mah, Reika Watanabe, Hailey M. Tanner, Troy Comi, Yuan Cai, Cheng-Yi Chen, Aartjan J. W. te Velthuis, Clifford P. Brangwynne, and Gene W. Yeo. This research received additional support from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, the Princeton Biomolecular Condensate Program, the Princeton Center for Complex Materials, the U.S. National Science Foundation Materials Research Science and Engineering Centers (NSF DMR-2011750), the St. Jude Collaborative on Membraneless Organelles, the AFOSR Multidisciplinary Research Program of the University Research Initiative (FA9550-20-1-0241), the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative Exploratory Cell Network, the National Institutes of Health (grant DP2 AI17547401), and the UC San Diego Sanford Stem Cell Institute. Fang was also supported by The Tullie and Rickey Families SPARK Awards for Innovations in Immunology, through the generosity of LJI Board Director Sandor Shapery and Rebecca Shapery, and a 2025 Omenn Darling Postdoctoral Fellowship through Princeton Bioengineering Institute. About La Jolla Institute La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) was founded in 1988 as an independent, nonprofit research organization. LJI is based in San Diego, CA, and is home to world-class scientists solely focused on immunology. LJI scientists are harnessing the power of the immune system to defeat cancer, autoimmune, infectious, and neurodegenerative diseases. Our breakthroughs in immunology make life without disease possible. Visit lji.org for more information. analysis.brief_en: A new study by scientists at the La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) and collaborators has uncovered a molecular reason why humans are uniquely vulnerable to severe Ebola disease. The research, published on November 19, 2026, reveals that Ebola virus forms membraneless condensates inside human cells, trapping specific human mRNA molecules and disrupting the immune system's ability to control inflammation. This leads to dangerous immune responses, causing organ failure and high fatality rates. In contrast, bats can carry the virus without getting sick, as their mRNA molecules adopt different folding features and are not trapped by the virus. The study highlights the critical role of these viral 'nests' in human disease severity. The current outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has already caused over 10,500 confirmed cases and over 5,130 deaths, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The findings are based on spatial transcriptomics methods and are not under investigation.

news.content_zh: 拉霍亚免疫学研究所 (LJI) 的科学家和合作者进行的一项新研究揭示了人类特别容易感染严重埃博拉疾病的分子原因。该研究于 2026 年 11 月 19 日发表,揭示 埃博拉病毒 在人体细胞内形成无膜凝聚物,捕获特定的人类 mRNA 分子并破坏免疫系统控制炎症的能力。这会导致危险的免疫应答,导致器官衰竭和高死亡率。相比之下,蝙蝠可以携带病毒而不生病,因为它们的 mRNA 分子具有不同的折叠特征,不会被病毒捕获。该研究强调了这些病毒“巢穴”在人类疾病严重程度中的关键作用。据美国疾病控制与预防中心称,目前刚果民主共和国的 暴发 已造成 10,500 多例确诊病例和 5,130 多人死亡。该发现基于空间转录组学方法,尚未进行调查。

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 25, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Bundibugyo Virus Disease Commonly Presents Without Haemorrhage in Outbreak Settings Review Finds by November 25, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Bundibugyo Virus Disease Commonly Presents Without Haemorrhage in Outbreak Settings Review Finds Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A structured clinical review updated through October 2026 documents that Bundibugyo virus disease manifests primarily as a nonspecific febrile and gastrointestinal condition rather than a visibly haemorrhagic fever in outbreak settings. The analysis evaluates patient care considerations amid the ongoing epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which has emerged as the largest recorded outbreak of Bundibugyo virus in history. According to surveillance figures from the World Health Organization cited in the assessment, the epidemic had reached 7,890 confirmed cases and 3,799 fatalities across 63 health zones in seven provinces by late September 2026. Bundibugyo virus was first recognized during an outbreak in western Uganda in 2007 and 2008, followed by a second documented outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2012. Because those historical outbreaks involved relatively small cohorts, considerable clinical uncertainty has persisted regarding disease progression, species-specific diagnostic performance, optimal supportive therapies, and the direct transferability of countermeasures developed for Ebola virus. The investigative team conducted a structured narrative synthesis covering evidence published up to October 1, 2026, across major medical databases including PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, the Cochrane Library, and the World Health Organization Global Index Medicus. Researchers paired operational terminology for Bundibugyo virus, Bundibugyo virus disease, and Ebola Bundibugyo with indexing headings addressing epidemiology, clinical features, diagnostic evaluation, supportive interventions, infection prevention, candidate vaccines, and therapeutic trials. The authors systematically augmented these database queries by incorporating official outbreak situation reports and clinical guidance issued by the World Health Organization, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, and the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
