news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 25, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Cross-Sectional Survey in Somaliland Finds Limited Prior Awareness of Ebola Disease by November 23, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Cross-Sectional Survey in Somaliland Finds Limited Prior Awareness of Ebola Disease Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram In an urban assessment of epidemic preparedness in the Horn of Africa, investigators surveying the commercial center of Burao, Somaliland, found that fewer than half of surveyed adult residents had ever heard of Ebola virus disease. The cross-sectional investigation, conducted across residential neighborhoods between June 2 and July 21, 2026, recruited 788 consenting adults to assess baseline awareness and evaluate how health communication functions in an urban center that has never recorded an Ebola outbreak. The findings demonstrate that in settings without documented transmission history, basic familiarity with high-consequence pathogens cannot be assumed, pointing to clear public communication priorities before an infectious threat emerges. Ebola virus disease is a severe zoonotic infection caused by viruses of the genus Orthoebolavirus, characterized by human-to-human transmission through direct contact with blood, body fluids, or contaminated materials from sick or deceased individuals. Effective containment during an active outbreak relies on early detection, clinical management, rigorous infection prevention, contact tracing, safe and dignified burial practices, targeted vaccination where appropriate, and sustained community cooperation. Because successful response measures depend on the willingness of residents to seek formal care and promptly report suspected cases, technical health-system capacity must be reinforced by community-level readiness to recognize transmission risks and follow public health advice. Although Somaliland had documented no Ebola virus disease transmission prior to the survey period, regional connectivity, trade links, and population movement make proactive preparedness essential for local health authorities. Somalia has made structural progress in expanding its integrated disease surveillance and response framework by introducing technical guidelines and electronic platforms such as the District Health Information Software 2, but implementation and sustained operational resources remain uneven. Prior preparedness research across African regions has repeatedly shown that general name recognition does not guarantee an accurate grasp of transmission pathways, as misconceptions regarding airborne spread, mosquito vectors, and survivor stigma often persist alongside broad awareness. To evaluate these dynamics systematically, researchers designed a community-based cross-sectional study targeting adult residents aged 18 years and older who had lived in Burao for at least six months. The administrative structure of Burao was used to identify residential zones, followed by proportional allocation across neighborhoods and systematic household sampling using a defined sampling interval after selecting a random starting dwelling. Within each selected household, a single eligible adult was chosen via the lottery method to give participants a defined probability of inclusion and minimize interviewer bias. The survey team utilized mobile electronic devices equipped with a bilingual Somali and English questionnaire programmed in KoboToolbox, featuring mandatory data fields, logical range limits, and automated skip logic to prevent incomplete or contradictory entries. A total of 810 adult contacts yielded 788 consenting respondents, among whom 591 were female and 464 were married, with an overall mean participant age of 33.8 years and an average household size of 7.4 persons. Of the 788 consenting adults, exactly 387 participants, representing 49.1 percent, reported that they had previously heard of Ebola virus disease, while 401 individuals, or 50.9 percent, had not. Under the study’s skip-logic protocol, only the 387 previously aware participants completed the detailed modules evaluating factual knowledge, attitudes, current preventive practices, and hypothetical outbreak responses. The 401 unaware adults were not administered these conditional sections, ensuring that downstream scores reflected only the subgroup with prior awareness rather than the broader community population. Multivariable modified Poisson regression analysis encompassing 780 complete-case records indicated that educational attainment was strongly linked to baseline disease recognition. Compared with respondents who had no formal education or religious instruction only, participants with primary or secondary schooling exhibited a higher adjusted prevalence of awareness, with an adjusted prevalence ratio of 1.34 and a 95 percent confidence interval spanning 1.09 to 1.64. Those with post-secondary education demonstrated an adjusted prevalence ratio of 1.87 with a 95 percent confidence interval between 1.52 and 2.31. Awareness was also more common among individuals reporting prior contact with someone from an outbreak-affected country, with an adjusted prevalence ratio of 1.22, and respondents working in high-contact occupations, with an adjusted prevalence ratio of 1.18. Among the 387 adults who had previously heard of the disease, detailed continuous scores revealed substantial variation in factual knowledge alongside generally cooperative attitudes. Knowledge was evaluated through 33 true-false statements spanning disease etiology, symptoms, transmission routes, reporting protocols, isolation, and common misconceptions, producing a mean knowledge score of 60.6 percent with a standard deviation of 24.1 and high internal consistency reflected by a Kuder-Richardson 20 coefficient of 0.928. Favorable attitudes, evaluated across 21 Likert items addressing institutional trust, perceived severity, survivor acceptance, and compliance with interventions, averaged 67.0 percent with a standard deviation of 14.0. Hypothetical intended responses across nine emergency scenarios averaged 73.3 percent with a standard deviation of 19.6, showing widespread stated willingness to report illnesses and accept medical guidance. In multivariable linear regression models examining 368 complete cases among the aware subgroup, specific educational exposures were independently associated with higher knowledge scores. Having received Ebola-related information within the preceding 12 months was associated with a 9.04 percentage-point increase in knowledge score, while formal educational instruction on Ebola was associated with an adjusted advantage of 12.97 percentage points. Knowledge scores were positively associated with favorable-attitude scores, which increased by 0.22 points for every one-point rise in knowledge. In turn, both knowledge and favorable attitudes were positively associated with hypothetical intended-response scores, with intended-response scores increasing by 1.01 points for each one-point increase in the favorable-attitude metric. Analysis of current observable behaviors among the 387 aware participants demonstrated that general protective actions were reported far more frequently than information-seeking activities. Specifically, 61.8 percent of respondents reported frequently avoiding unprotected contact with blood or body fluids, and 61.2 percent reported frequently washing hands after caring for an ill individual. Conversely, only 41.9 percent reported routinely verifying health information before sharing it, and only 37.5 percent had actively sought reliable information on Ebola virus disease during the preceding six months. When assessing general perceptions across all 788 consenting adults, 50.6 percent believed local health facilities were equipped to identify and manage suspected cases, 48.5 percent agreed that residents knew where to report cases, and 76.4 percent agreed that the community required additional education regarding the disease. The study authors emphasized several critical methodological limitations that frame the interpretation of these findings. Because the cross-sectional design collects exposures and outcomes concurrently, observed statistical associations cannot confirm causal relationships or determine whether educational exposure directly improved awareness. Furthermore, knowledge, attitude, and behavioral estimates describe exclusively the 387 adults who had already heard of the disease, and these scores cannot be interpreted as community-wide averages or validated measures of operational readiness. Survey records lacked full primary sampling unit identifiers and household inclusion probabilities, precluding design-weighted national population estimates, while the favorable-attitude linear model exhibited evidence of functional-form misspecification under specification testing. Consequently, the researchers concluded that proactive preparedness in Burao must focus on plain-language, bilingual outreach delivered through radio, religious venues, and educational institutions to reach individuals outside formal educational networks before alerts occur. Beyond summary averages, researchers analyzed score categorizations and individual behaviors to evaluate preparedness nuances. When categorizing knowledge scores into pragmatic descriptive tiers, 138 participants (35.7 percent) scored below 60 percent, 188 (48.6 percent) fell between 60 and 80 percent, and 61 (15.8 percent) reached at least 80 percent. In separate modified Poisson models examining observable daily practices, formal education on the disease significantly increased the likelihood of positive actions among the previously aware group. Specifically, individuals with formal instruction were more likely to actively seek reliable information (adjusted prevalence ratio 2.54, 95 percent confidence interval 1.86 to 3.47), discuss protective practices with household members (adjusted prevalence ratio 1.46, 95 percent confidence interval 1.18 to 1.81), and verify health information before sharing it (adjusted prevalence ratio 1.27, 95 percent confidence interval 1.01 to 1.60). Across the nine hypothetical emergency scenarios, intended cooperation remained consistently high, spanning from 70.5 percent for adhering to physical contact restrictions up to 78.3 percent for advising an ill neighbor to seek medical care. To test the stability of their linear regression findings, the investigators conducted multiple sensitivity checks addressing clustering and outcome boundaries. Re-estimating the primary models using standard errors clustered across 54 recorded interviewers affirmed the positive relationships between recent disease information, formal training, knowledge, and favorable attitudes. Additionally, because percentage scores are inherently bounded, researchers fitted fractional logistic generalized linear models, which yielded average marginal contrasts pointing in the same direction. An exploratory nonlinear sensitivity analysis incorporating cubic splines for age and knowledge revealed that attitude gains were not strictly uniform across the knowledge distribution; predicted attitude score increases per ten-point rise in knowledge expanded from 1.06 points at the lower end of the scale to 3.93 points at higher knowledge levels. Public engagement preferences and perceived obstacles highlighted specific avenues for community-level intervention. Beyond general support for health education, 494 participants (62.7 percent) agreed that rumors and social stigma represented substantial barriers to outbreak control. When assessing trusted communication formats across all 788 respondents, institutional channels received broad backing: 74.1 percent favored schools and universities, 72.7 percent endorsed Somali-language radio broadcasts, 71.3 percent supported official updates from health authorities, and 67.6 percent preferred outreach through mosques or religious leaders. Specifically, individuals with formal instruction were more likely to actively seek reliable information (adjusted prevalence ratio 2.54, 95 percent confidence interval 1.86 to 3.47), discuss protective practices with household members (adjusted prevalence ratio 1.46, 95 percent confidence interval 1.18 to 1.81), and verify health information before sharing it (adjusted prevalence ratio 1.27, 95 percent confidence interval 1.01 to 1.60). Across the nine hypothetical emergency scenarios, intended cooperation remained consistently high, spanning from 70.5 percent for adhering to physical contact restrictions up to 78.3 percent for advising an ill neighbor to seek medical care. To test the stability of their linear regression findings, the investigators conducted multiple sensitivity checks addressing clustering and outcome boundaries. Re-estimating the primary models using standard errors clustered across 54 recorded interviewers affirmed the positive relationships between recent disease information, formal training, knowledge, and favorable attitudes. Additionally, because percentage scores are inherently bounded, researchers fitted fractional logistic generalized linear models, which yielded average marginal contrasts pointing in the same direction. An exploratory nonlinear sensitivity analysis incorporating cubic splines for age and knowledge revealed that attitude gains were not strictly uniform across the knowledge distribution; predicted attitude score increases per ten-point rise in knowledge expanded from 1.06 points at the lower end of the scale to 3.93 points at higher knowledge levels. Public engagement preferences and perceived obstacles highlighted specific avenues for community-level intervention. Beyond general support for health education, 494 participants (62.7 percent) agreed that rumors and social stigma represented substantial barriers to outbreak control. When assessing trusted communication formats across all 788 respondents, institutional channels received broad backing: 74.1 percent favored schools and universities, 72.7 percent endorsed Somali-language radio broadcasts, 71.3 percent supported official updates from health authorities, and 67.6 percent preferred outreach through mosques or religious leaders. analysis.time: The survey was conducted between June 2 and July 21, 2026, with the news published on November 23, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The study took place in Burao, Somaliland, focusing on adult residents aged 18 years and older who had lived there for at least six months. The survey included 788 consenting adults, with 591 females and 464 married individuals, averaging 33.8 years of age and 7.4 persons per household.
analysis.event: A cross-sectional survey in Burao, Somaliland, found that 49.1 percent of surveyed adults had prior awareness of Ebola virus disease, while 50.9 percent had not. The survey aimed to assess baseline awareness and health communication effectiveness in an area without documented Ebola outbreaks.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The survey revealed limited public awareness of Ebola virus disease, with 50.9 percent of adults unaware. This highlights the need for improved health communication and community preparedness, as effective containment during an outbreak depends on early detection, clinical management, and community cooperation. The study also showed that educational attainment and prior contact with outbreak-affected countries were associated with higher awareness.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The survey was conducted to evaluate public awareness and preparedness, and the findings suggest that community-level readiness is essential for effective outbreak response. The study used systematic sampling, electronic questionnaires, and statistical analysis to assess knowledge, attitudes, and hypothetical responses. However, no confirmed cases or outbreaks were reported in the area, and the results are based on self-reported awareness rather than actual disease transmission.

news.content: Sign InSubscribeView Basket Sign InSubscribeView Basket *** DEBUG START *** *** DEBUG END *** Wednesday 25 November 2026 Home UK World Comment Opinion Analysis Columnists Leader comment Letters to the editor Features Features Interviews Faith Faith features Articles of faith Theology matters In the parish Sunday’s readings Prayer for the week Faith for Holy Places The Mystery of Faith Books & Arts Book reviews New titles Film Podcast reviews Art Music Performing Arts TV Radio Regulars Gazette Cartoons Caption competition Crossword Notebook 100 years ago Quotes Holidays Links Audio & Video Podcast Video Archive Jobs Events Home UK World Comment Opinion Analysis Columnists Leader comment Letters to the editor Features Features Interviews Faith Faith features Articles of faith Theology matters In the parish Sunday’s readings Prayer for the week Faith for Holy Places The Mystery of Faith Books & Arts Book reviews New titles Film Podcast reviews Art Music Performing Arts TV Radio Regulars Gazette Cartoons Caption competition Crossword Notebook 100 years ago Quotes Holidays Links Audio & Video Podcast Video Archive Jobs Events Ebola virus now ‘out of control’ in the Democratic Republic of the Congo by Rebecca Paveley 20 November 2026 Health agencies warn that an Ebola outbreak in the DRC is out of control Alamy Patients celebrate after recovering from the Ebola virus at treatment centre in Beni, in the eastern DRC, last month Patients celebrate after recovering from the Ebola virus at treatment centre in Beni, in the eastern DRC, last month 0:00 / 0:00 THE Ebola virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is spreading faster and proving more deadly than in earlier outbreaks, and health agencies are now warning that it is out of control. Delayed detection, ongoing conflict, overstretched health services, and shortages of medical equipment and trained staff have hampered efforts to contain the disease. The outbreak, declared in May, is caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which there is no vaccine. In the DRC alone, there have been 11,376 confirmed cases and 5,568 deaths; there are also a few cases in neighbouring countries. The outbreak of 2014-16, which killed about 11,000 people, was the worst previously recorded globally. In the DRC, about half of the patients infected are dying. Among the under-fives who have contracted the virus, the proportion rises to 72 per cent, UNICEF says. The outbreak “is serious, and is not under control”, the director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control, Jean Kaseya, told Reuters. “If we don’t stop this outbreak now, it would be the worst Ebola outbreak that the world will have.” The charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said this week that international aid was failing to reach areas where it was most needed, and blamed the lack of trained and paid staff, fuel for ambulances, and supplies to manage suspected cases. It said that there was a “troubling disconnect” between resources promised and what was reaching patients and communities. “Despite the vast amounts of money provided for the response, many front-line responders are left trying to contain the outbreak with empty hands and empty pockets,” MSF’s international president, Dr Javid Abdelmoneim, said. “Our teams are often left speechless by the dysfunctions they witness in many areas. Six months into the response, this situation is simply unacceptable.” Beyond the DRC, Uganda was the first country to report cases in this outbreak. It recorded 20 confirmed cases and two deaths, almost all involving people who had travelled from the DRC, and was declared free of the virus in August. Advertisement Kenya has identified nine cases. Two patients died and seven others recovered. The last was discharged from hospital last week. Tearfund is providing personal protective equipment and handwashing equipment in the DRC. The charity is also supporting survivors, many of whom have been left with long-term health effects, known as “post-Ebola syndrome”. The charity is also working with communities to address misinformation and mistrust. Healthcare workers have faced threats and violence from fearful communities, and shortages of protective equipment have left them at risk. Many healthcare workers have not been paid since the outbreak was declared in May. Henri, a healthcare worker at a treatment centre, is being supported by Tearfund. He said: “I am a nurse. We had been working at the Ebola Treatment Centre for more than two months when I eventually became infected. At the beginning of the outbreak, when suspected cases first began arriving at the hospital, we were genuinely afraid. Every member of staff was afraid to care for those patients. We imagined all sorts of things. We wondered whether we would become infected there. Health workers are also on the front line. “We had treated this disease, we had suffered from it, and we had been treated ourselves. We could not abandon other patients. That is why we found the courage to continue caring for them.” Henri said that the financial assistance provided through Tearfund would help him and his family, after several weeks of illness had stopped him from working. “The assistance Tearfund is providing will make a real difference in meeting my needs. I have not yet been able to buy all my children’s school supplies. And because I was ill for several weeks, this assistance will also help me resume my farming work.” Browse Church and Charity jobs on the Church Times jobsite Other stories Ebola virus a growing challenge in Africa 30 Oct 2026 Children in DRC more likely to die from Ebola than adults, aid agencies warn 18 Jun 2026 Fear and unrest as rare strain of Ebola virus in DRC spreads 27 May 2026 Clergy courage in DRC Ebola crisis praised 05 Jun 2026 Ebola deaths surge to 1,400 in the DRC 31 Jul 2026 Anglican Primates plead for peace in the DRC 21 Feb 2025 World COP31 talks draw to a close 20 Nov 2026 Church groups back Spanish general strike 16 Nov 2026 Hungary moves to relax regulations on abortion 20 Nov 2026 World news in brief 20 Nov 2026 Jordan’s Christmas to be low-key 20 Nov 2026 COP31: vulnerable nations call for clarity about plans for adaptation finance 13 Nov 2026 Other Topics UKBooks & ArtsFaith VIEW A SAMPLE COPY Subscribe Top Comment There is no single story to tell about ‘the north’ Beware of simplistic, romantic narratives about the Province: the reality is much more complicated, argues Jenni Beaumont jobs.CHURCHTIMES Job of the Week Team Rector London and Home Counties The Bishop of Fulham seeks to appoint a Full Stipend Vicar for the Benefice of St Michael, Wood Green with St Gabriel, Bounds Green and St Michael-at-Bowes. Delayed detection, ongoing conflict, overstretched health services, and shortages of medical equipment and trained staff have hampered efforts to contain the disease. The outbreak, declared in May, is caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which there is no vaccine. In the DRC alone, there have been 11,376 confirmed cases and 5,568 deaths; there are also a few cases in neighbouring countries. The outbreak of 2014-16, which killed about 11,000 people, was the worst previously recorded globally. In the DRC, about half of the patients infected are dying. Among the under-fives who have contracted the virus, the proportion rises to 72 per cent, UNICEF says. The outbreak “is serious, and is not under control”, the director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control, Jean Kaseya, told Reuters. “If we don’t stop this outbreak now, it would be the worst Ebola outbreak that the world will have.” The charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said this week that international aid was failing to reach areas where it was most needed, and blamed the lack of trained and paid staff, fuel for ambulances, and supplies to manage suspected cases. It said that there was a “troubling disconnect” between resources promised and what was reaching patients and communities. “Despite the vast amounts of money provided for the response, many front-line responders are left trying to contain the outbreak with empty hands and empty pockets,” MSF’s international president, Dr Javid Abdelmoneim, said. “Our teams are often left speechless by the dysfunctions they witness in many areas. Six months into the response, this situation is simply unacceptable.” Beyond the DRC, Uganda was the first country to report cases in this outbreak. It recorded 20 confirmed cases and two deaths, almost all involving people who had travelled from the DRC, and was declared free of the virus in August. Advertisement Kenya has identified nine cases. Two patients died and seven others recovered. The last was discharged from hospital last week. Tearfund is providing personal protective equipment and handwashing equipment in the DRC. The charity is also supporting survivors, many of whom have been left with long-term health effects, known as “post-Ebola syndrome”. The charity is also working with communities to address misinformation and mistrust. Healthcare workers have faced threats and violence from fearful communities, and shortages of protective equipment have left them at risk. Many healthcare workers have not been paid since the outbreak was declared in May. Henri, a healthcare worker at a treatment centre, is being supported by Tearfund. He said: “I am a nurse. We had been working at the Ebola Treatment Centre for more than two months when I eventually became infected. At the beginning of the outbreak, when suspected cases first began arriving at the hospital, we were genuinely afraid. Every member of staff was afraid to care for those patients. We imagined all sorts of things. We wondered whether we would become infected there. Health workers are also on the front line. “We had treated this disease, we had suffered from it, and we had been treated ourselves. We could not abandon other patients. That is why we found the courage to continue caring for them.” Henri said that the financial assistance provided through Tearfund would help him and his family, after several weeks of illness had stopped him from working. “The assistance Tearfund is providing will make a real difference in meeting my needs. I have not yet been able to buy all my children’s school supplies. news.content: Menu Listen Live News Weather Cancellations Events Obituaries Blogs & Podcasts Blogs Podcasts On Air × Sign In Search News Weather Cancellations Events Obituaries Blogs & Podcasts Blogs Podcasts On Air Analysis-Scientists are learning more about the rare Ebola virus in Congo outbreak By Thomson Reuters Nov 20, 2026 | 6:06 AM By Jennifer Rigby LONDON, Nov 20 (Reuters) – More than six months into a devastating Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, scientists and medics are beginning to gain a better understanding of the rare Bundibugyo version of the virus, which they hope can help explain its rapid spread and, ultimately, stop it. There have been more than 11,000 cases and over 5,500 deaths so far, with the Bundibugyo virus spreading at double the pace of the 2014-2016 Ebola outbreak in West Africa, the largest on record. There are no licensed treatments or vaccines to fight it. The outbreak’s location in a part of ‌eastern Congo already facing a humanitarian crisis could be complicating what scientists are finding, several experts said, and cautioned against drawing early conclusions as data is limited, varied and often difficult to collect. “There are so many different factors to compare across outbreaks, even within outbreaks — it is really hard,” said Daniel Bausch, a member of the World Health Organization’s Ebola emergency committee and visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute in Switzerland. Catherine Smallwood, the WHO’s Ebola incident manager, said teams were gathering evidence to help better inform the response. “Soon we’ll be able to make some bold statements about what’s the same, what’s different, and what we ‌need to adjust,” she said. BLEEDING LESS COMMON A key area of investigation centers on Bundibugyo’s symptoms, particularly in children, WHO and Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention officials told Reuters. Infection with Ebola can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding. But bleeding is only occurring in around 5% to 10% of confirmed cases in the Bundibugyo outbreak, said Yap Boum, Africa CDC’s deputy Ebola incident manager, making it less common than in outbreaks of the more prevalent Ebola, Zaire. This makes the disease easier to confuse with other more common illnesses like malaria, which Boum said could have contributed to the late detection of the outbreak alongside early challenges with diagnosis, as the tests designed for other Ebola species do not pick up Bundibugyo. It is also making it harder to track the spread, as many people do not suspect Ebola and seek care. Around 70% of patients are still dying in their communities rather than in healthcare centres. While the outbreak was declared in May, the WHO and Africa CDC believe transmission may have been occurring months before that. Jean-Jacques Muyembe, co-discoverer of Ebola and the head of Congo’s National Institute for Biomedical Research, said bleeding was also occurring later in the disease for some patients. Bausch said many scientists now think bleeding is less of a hallmark symptom of all Ebola disease than they used to based on data gathered over years, although it seems even more rare for Bundibugyo patients. RISK TO CHILDREN In young children, the situation is even more complex, said the WHO’s Smallwood. Gastrointestinal symptoms are more common than fever, complicating early diagnosis and ‌treatment, which could also be a reason why children are being disproportionately affected, she said. There have been 1,207 confirmed cases of Ebola in children under the age of 5, and 844 of them have died, roughly 7 in 10, according to the latest data from the Congolese ministry of health and the WHO. That is higher than among adults, for whom the fatality rate is around 50%, which is above previous Bundibugyo outbreaks but below the typical rates for Zaire, Muyembe and other types of Ebola, which can be up to 80% without treatment. REMAINING QUESTIONS There are still many questions that need further study, half-a-dozen leading experts said, including how common it is for patients to experience mild symptoms, as well as the long-term implications of infection for survivors. Around 700 survivors have enrolled in a study and support schemes, the WHO said. Genomic sequencing, which previously found distinct differences from more common Ebola viruses, shows Bundibugyo is not changing rapidly or becoming more transmissible. But Sylvie Jonckheere, Médecins ‌Sans Frontières’ emerging and reemerging infectious diseases adviser, said research remained a challenge when so many cases were still not being identified before victims die in the community. “If we don’t find the ones that are severely sick, what is our hope of finding the ‌ones that are only mildly sick?” she said. Prompt access to good care massively improves the chance of survival, the experts said. Several experts noted that progress in stamping out the outbreak in some of the early hotspots demonstrated that standard control measures, like isolating patients, do work. Like Zaire, this virus seems only to transmit when patients are symptomatic. But the big research question remains what vaccines and treatments could be effective. A trial of Merck’s Ervebo vaccine, developed to prevent Zaire, is assessing whether it might offer cross-protection for Bundibugyo. New vaccines developed for Bundibugyo specifically will also enter trials soon, and medics are testing prophylactic antivirals and treatments in Congo from Gilead Sciences and Mapp Biopharmaceutical. “When we started, we said there are no vaccines, no treatments,” Boum said. “If we start proving we have some efficacy... it becomes a game changer.” (Reporting by Jennifer Rigby; Additional reporting by Clément Bonnerot in Dakar; Editing by Caroline Humer and Bill Berkrot) Comments Leave a Reply Cancel reply You must be logged in to post a comment. Bausch said many scientists now think bleeding is less of a hallmark symptom of all Ebola disease than they used to based on data gathered over years, although it seems even more rare for Bundibugyo patients. analysis.brief_en: In the Democratic Republic of Congo, a Bundibugyo virus outbreak has been ongoing for more than six months, with over 11,000 cases and over 5,500 deaths reported. Scientists are working to understand the virus's behavior, particularly its symptoms and transmission patterns, as it spreads at double the rate of the 2014-2016 West African outbreak. The outbreak is occurring in a region already affected by a humanitarian crisis, complicating efforts to track and respond. Notably, bleeding is less common in this outbreak compared to other Ebola strains, which may lead to misdiagnosis and delayed detection. The situation highlights the need for improved diagnostic tools and better access to healthcare to reduce mortality and control the spread of the virus.

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 25, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Uganda Rapidly Contained an Urban Sudan Virus Disease Outbreak Within 87 Days by November 19, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Uganda Rapidly Contained an Urban Sudan Virus Disease Outbreak Within 87 Days Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A retrospective implementation analysis published in the Journal of Epidemiology and Global Health reveals how public health authorities in Uganda successfully interrupted transmission of an urban Sudan virus disease outbreak within 87 days. The outbreak, declared by the Uganda Ministry of Health on January 30, 2025, after laboratory confirmation across three independent national reference laboratories, emerged in Kampala, one of East Africa’s most densely populated and interconnected metropolitan hubs. Despite severe constraints that included major disruptions to global health financing and the total absence of licensed vaccines or targeted therapeutics for Sudan ebolavirus, the outbreak was limited to 14 total cases across seven districts. Two deaths occurred among confirmed cases, yielding a confirmed-case fatality rate of 16.7 percent, while all confirmed patients who were admitted to designated Ebola Treatment Units survived under optimized supportive clinical care protocols. The outbreak initially presented significant risks of rapid community amplification and cross-regional transmission due to the unique profile of the index case. The primary detected individual was a 32-year-old male nurse working at Mulago National Referral Hospital, an urban medical facility in Kampala with a capacity exceeding 1,500 beds that routinely serves patients, attendants, and visitors from across the nation. The patient developed symptoms on January 19, 2025, continued to work while symptomatic, and traveled through several districts before succumbing to the illness on January 29, 2025. Although intensive multi-sectoral retrospective and prospective field investigations were conducted under the National One Health Platform, the original zoonotic spillover event could not be ascertained, and the precise source of infection remained unidentified. The lack of documented travel outside Kampala and Wakiso prior to symptom onset meant investigators could not establish whether the healthcare worker acquired the pathogen occupationally, underscoring that he represented the first detected case rather than a confirmed primary spillover event. Discover more Check Symptoms Track Outbreaks Study Biology To evaluate the operational mechanics behind the containment, investigators structured a retrospective review of official documentation spanning the entire 87-day intervention through the formal declaration of the outbreak’s end on April 26, 2025. The research team systematically examined national and district response plans, standard operating procedures, daily situation reports produced by the Public Health Emergency Operations Centre, laboratory summaries, and formal after-action review documents. The analysis benchmarked actual implementation performance against the World Health Organization Strategic Preparedness and Response Plan framework and the international 7-1-7 timeliness metrics. While the detection of the index case took 10 days from symptom onset—narrowly missing the 7-day target because initial clinical suspicion had not identified the infection prior to postmortem sampling—official notification occurred in under 24 hours, and coordinated emergency operations across all operational pillars launched on the very first day. Discover more Buy Maps Read Travel Guides Shop African Art Find Treatments A central novel pillar of the containment strategy was the deployment of mandatory institutional quarantine for all identified contacts rather than relying on home-based monitoring. In previous Ugandan filovirus responses, including the 2022 Sudan virus disease outbreak that spread across rural and peri-urban districts, quarantine was primarily restricted to suspected cases while known contacts remained under home observation. Recognizing the severe hazards posed by Kampala’s day-time population of over 2.5 million people and an extended metropolitan area surpassing 4.49 million residents, the National Task Force and Incident Management Team mandated institutional supervision under powers granted by Uganda’s Public Health Act. A total of 491 contacts were line-listed and systematically monitored for the full 21-day incubation window using the digital Go.Data platform. Over 95 percent of these identified individuals were accommodated directly within Mulago National Referral Hospital, designated hotels, and contracted guest houses, ensuring that contacts who developed active disease were already separated from the public. The effectiveness of mandatory institutional containment was directly reflected in the downstream transmission patterns documented by the surveillance teams. Of the 14 total cases recorded across the outbreak, only two arose from unrecognized community transmission, whereas the remaining 12 cases emerged among previously traced and isolated contacts who had been evacuated into monitored facilities before wider exposures could occur. Six of these secondary cases were healthcare workers who had shared clinical environments or household quarters with the index patient. Because contacts were closely evaluated around the clock, individuals exhibiting early symptoms were transferred without delay to clinical isolation units, diagnosed, and placed on supportive therapies. Breaking transmission chains through supervised institutional quarantine averted uncontrolled urban spread and prevented the secondary community clustering that had prolonged historical outbreaks. Another defining operational innovation was the systemic detection of cases through routine and intensified mortality surveillance. Because approximately two thirds of deaths in the country occur within local communities rather than formal clinical wards, the surveillance pillar collected and evaluated 2,945 postmortem diagnostic samples from non-traumatic deaths in both healthcare facilities and community settings. Testing was performed across independent reference laboratories using standardized viral hemorrhagic fever panels. This mortality surveillance infrastructure directly identified the index case postmortem following his death at Mulago Hospital and subsequently detected a second fatal confirmed case. Identifying deceased cases through postmortem diagnostic channels prompted instantaneous epidemiological ring investigations and prevented unsafe customary burial practices, which historically represent primary drivers of amplification during filovirus emergencies. Laboratory and diagnostic systems demonstrated substantial capacity gains through the decentralization of mobile testing facilities and the integration of rapid district response units. While initial index-case verification required 12 hours from sample delivery to coordinate concordant testing across three independent national reference laboratories, the forward deployment of a specialized mobile laboratory to Mbale District on January 31 reduced subsequent diagnostic turnaround times to approximately six hours. Accompanied by dedicated district laboratory response teams and national sample-referral transport hubs, these mobile platforms allowed clinicians to confirm or rule out suspected infections rapidly in outlying districts such as Mbale and Kyegegwa. Concurrently, domestic genomic sequencing capabilities were deployed to trace viral lineages and characterize linkages among confirmed cases, providing real-time epidemiological verification across transmission chains. The clinical management pillar delivered supportive care guided by the World Health Organization optimized supportive care framework, achieving a zero percent mortality rate among all confirmed cases admitted to treatment facilities. Six specialized clinical care experts and 78 Emergency Medical Team personnel staffed treatment centers equipped with prepositioned infection prevention and control infrastructure. In contrast to the 2022 outbreak—where at least 19 healthcare workers contracted the virus and seven died—no health worker involved in the 2025 clinical response acquired infection. Beyond standard rehydration, electrolyte management, and organ support, patients accessed investigational antivirals including remdesivir within a randomized clinical trial framework. Discharged patients transitioned into a dedicated survivor program that conducted regular testing of bodily fluids to monitor viral shedding, provided risk-reduction counseling including condom distribution to prevent potential sexual transmission, and delivered structured psychological support. Emergency clinical research platforms were mobilized with unprecedented speed, highlighted by the initiation of the Tokemeza SVD ring-vaccination trial on February 3, 2025, just four days following the official outbreak declaration. Sponsoring organizations including Makerere University Lung Institute, the Uganda Virus Research Institute, and the Ministry of Health leveraged standing regulatory approvals, pre-cleared ethical authorizations, and established standby protocols developed following the 2022 epidemic. Concurrently, risk communication and community engagement teams embedded social anthropologists directly into field response units to conduct systematic participant observation and social listening in identified hotspots. By identifying public anxieties, rumors, and specific grievances regarding quarantine conditions, the anthropologists guided the daily tailoring of 52,200 information products distributed across five local languages, engaging 1,555 Village Health Teams and broadcasting through local radio networks to reach an estimated audience of over 4.8 million individuals. These operational achievements were accomplished despite severe financial headwinds caused by global health financing disruptions and international funding freezes. The national emergency response operated under an acute financing deficit, securing only 29 percent of its required budget—amounting to approximately 16 million United States dollars out of an estimated 56 million dollar need. Critical operational pillars including surveillance, community engagement, and case management confronted funding deficits exceeding 70 percent, resulting in localized sample transit delays and responder stipend backlogs. This digital tracking tool minimized duplicate investments and directed scarce partner assets efficiently, while Uganda’s permanent investments in domestic reference infrastructure, designated isolation wards, and trained personnel substantially lowered the marginal cost of containment. The researchers emphasize several critical methodological and contextual limitations when interpreting these findings. Because the outbreak involved a small total cohort of 14 cases, observational data cannot statistically isolate the precise individual contribution of each intervention, such as distinguishing whether 100 percent treatment-unit survival resulted from advanced clinical care, the administration of investigational antivirals, or earlier patient presentation. Furthermore, intrinsic epidemiological dynamics, including a potentially low baseline reproduction number or circumscribed contact networks around the index case, may have contributed to rapid containment independently of operational interventions. The authors also acknowledge that Uganda’s extensive historical experience spanning 11 prior filovirus outbreaks provided an exceptional institutional foundation that may not be directly generalizable to lower-resource settings lacking standing laboratory networks, established emergency legislation, or pre-approved trial infrastructure. It resulted in 14 total cases and two confirmed deaths, with a fatality rate of 16.7 percent. Despite challenges such as limited global health financing and the absence of licensed vaccines, Uganda's public health authorities implemented a containment strategy that included mandatory institutional quarantine for contacts, systematic monitoring of 491 individuals using the Go.Data platform, and genomic sequencing to trace viral lineages. The outbreak was limited to seven districts, and all confirmed patients who were admitted to Ebola Treatment Units survived under optimized supportive care. The index case, a 32-year-old male nurse at Mulago National Referral Hospital, developed symptoms on January 19, 2025, and traveled through several districts before succumbing to the illness on January 29, 2025. The containment efforts were coordinated under the National One Health Platform, and the outbreak was officially declared over on April 26, 2025. The study also benchmarked Uganda's response against international frameworks, including the World Health Organization Strategic Preparedness and Response Plan and the 7-1-7 timeliness metrics.

news.content: Securing the future: CEPI's 3.0 Investment Case Find out moreDismiss About What we do Partner with us Our impact News & stories Contact us Blog Roadmap to accelerate access to Bundibugyo virus vaccines published CEPI19th November 2026 Share Vaccines to protect against Bundibugyo virus disease are being developed urgently, in support of the nationally led response to the current outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. For safe and effective vaccines to reach the people who need them as quickly as possible, planning for post-trial access must happen alongside research and development, not after it. That means planning in advance across the access spectrum, from the regulatory and policy pathways that enable access through to manufacturing, financing and delivery considerations. To support this planning, the interim Medical Countermeasures network (i-MCM-net) within the Vaccine Pillar of the Continental Incident Management Support Team has developed a Vaccine Access Roadmap. The document was co-developed by the Vaccine Pillar partners: Africa CDC, CEPI, Gavi, WHO (HQ and AFRO) and UNICEF, with multiple other stakeholders informing its development. The Roadmap maps the pathway to equitable access, identifies the known roles & responsibilities across the ecosystem, and highlights the most critical access priorities. Its aim is to give all vaccine response partners a shared approach to access. That way, R&D progress can be translated rapidly into accessible, suitable and implementable vaccination in Bundibugyo virus-affected communities. The Roadmap makes the following recommendations for governments, vaccine response partners and funders to accelerate access to Bundibugyo virus vaccines: Sustain clinical trial momentum and include special populations so they are not excluded from timely access. Continue to prioritise risk communication and community engagement and integrate social and behavioural science into trials and beyond. Prepare urgently for any expanded access or compassionate use of vaccines. Streamline regulatory pathways and outline sequencing and conditions for national and global regulatory authorisations. Ensure that product liability and indemnification (I&L) is not a barrier to across different regulatory scenarios. Incorporate programmatic suitability considerations into vaccine funding decisions. Define and communicate assumptions around an allocation mechanism for potential future vaccines should the outbreak expand beyond the DRC. Ensure country-level operational readiness to authorize, receive, deliver and administer vaccine doses. Integrate special access approaches for humanitarian populations of concern. Continue efforts to improve country-level active surveillance and community listening systems. A high-level summary in English and French and the full roadmap in English and French are available to download. Feedback from stakeholders is welcome at abd@cepi.net CEPI and World Bank Group partner to strengthen sustainable vaccine manufacturing in ASEAN Tracking Lassa fever: Where are we up to? 100 days into the Bundibugyo emergency, unprecedented speed is still not enough Where to go next Equitable accessRead moreEbola BundibugyoRead moreResearch and development Read moreThe 100 Days MissionRead more

news.content_zh: CEPI 与 疫苗 支柱合作伙伴(包括非洲疾病预防控制中心、全球疫苗和免疫联盟、世界卫生组织和联合国儿童基金会)合作,发布了一份路线图,以加速获得本迪布焦病毒的 疫苗。该文件于 2026 年 11 月 19 日发布,概述了为政府、疫苗 响应合作伙伴和资助者提供的关键建议,以确保公平的 疫苗 分配。其中包括维持临床试验势头、优先考虑风险沟通以及为扩大准入做好准备。该路线图强调需要简化监管途径和国家级授权、接收和交付 疫苗 的操作准备。它没有提供具体的病例或死亡人数,但强调了在受本迪布焦病毒影响的社区中快速且可访问的 疫苗接种 的重要性。该路线图是支持国家主导应对刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 正在进行的 暴发 的更广泛努力的一部分。

View 2 Images Health checks are taking place in neighbouring countries, such as the Central African Republic (Image: AFP via Getty Images) To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed. ‌ READ MORE: Two arrested after William and Kate's Sandringham home 'broken into by intruders' READ MORE: Gatwick Airport drop-off parking hacked as drivers warned bank details may have been stolen Dr Mohamed Janabi, the WHO’s Regional Director for Africa, told the Metro: "Insecurity, population movement, and transmission in hard-to-reach areas is making it harder to break the chains of transmission. "As long as the outbreak continues to spread further, I have to say that spread [internationally] is possible". ‌ A small number of Ebola cases have been recorded in Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria this year, while a British doctor was flown back home earlier this month after contracting the virus while working in the DRC. But the virus is yet to sustain continued transmission outside DR Congo, with both Kenya and Nigeria currently on track to declare their outbreaks over. ‌ Despite the outbreak being declared by the WHO in May, recent genetic sequencing revealed that the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola actually began spreading in Ituri province around February - putting health workers on the back foot in the spring when it came to containing it. There remains no cure for the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, though an experimental vaccine developed by the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India is currently being trialled in the DR Congo. ‌ It came as WHO staff and Ebola responders remained trapped inside a hospital maternity ward in Ituri province after intense fighting broke out at the weekend. The World Health Organisation said it hoped to rescue the group today after being delayed by heavy rain yesterday. Article continues below A spokesperson told reporters at the WHO's headquarters in Geneva: "Conflict as well as torrential rain yesterday meant that we were not able to move them safely. We’re hoping to do this as soon as possible, ideally today". analysis.time: The outbreak was declared in May 2026, with recent genetic sequencing indicating the Bundibugyo strain began spreading in Ituri province around February 2026. The WHO issued its warning on 2026-11-24.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak is primarily in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo), specifically in Ituri province. Cases have also been recorded in Uganda, Kenya, and Nigeria, though these are not sustained.
analysis.event: The World Health Organisation (WHO) warned that the 'unprecedented' Ebola outbreak could spread globally due to factors like insecurity, population movement, and transmission in hard-to-reach areas. The Bundibugyo strain of Ebola is the focus of the outbreak, with confirmed cases in DR Congo and some in neighboring countries.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Over 5,600 people have died since the outbreak was declared in May 2026. The number of confirmed cases is 11,793, but officials believe the true figure is higher due to underreporting and civil conflict. The WHO considers this outbreak the worst on record, and while there are no confirmed sustained transmissions outside DR Congo, the risk of international spread remains possible.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The WHO is conducting genetic sequencing and has initiated health checks in neighboring countries. However, the outbreak has been hampered by civil conflict and heavy rain, delaying rescue efforts for WHO staff trapped in a hospital maternity ward. The experimental vaccine by the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India is being trialled in DR Congo.

analysis.brief_en: The World Health Organisation (WHO) has issued a warning that the 'unprecedented' Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) could spread globally. The Bundibugyo strain of the virus, which was declared in May 2026, has caused over 5,600 deaths and 11,793 confirmed cases, though the actual numbers are likely higher due to underreporting and ongoing civil conflict. The WHO's top doctor highlighted that insecurity, population movement, and transmission in hard-to-reach areas pose significant challenges to containment. While some cases have been recorded in Uganda, Kenya, and Nigeria, these are not yet sustained. The outbreak is considered the worst on record, and the risk of international spread remains possible. Health checks are being conducted in neighboring countries, and an experimental vaccine is being trialled in DR Congo. Rescue efforts for WHO staff trapped in a hospital maternity ward in Ituri province have been delayed by heavy rain, and the WHO hopes to resolve the situation as soon as possible.

analysis_zh.location_and_population: 暴发 主要位于刚果民主共和国 (DR Congo),特别是伊图里省。乌干达、肯尼亚和尼日利亚也有病例记录,但这些情况并不持续。
analysis_zh.event: 世界卫生组织(WHO)警告称,由于不安全、人口流动和难以到达地区等因素,“前所未有”的埃博拉病毒可能在全球范围内传播。埃博拉病毒本迪布焦株是 暴发 的重点,在刚果民主共和国和邻国都有确诊病例。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 自2026年5月宣布暴发以来,已有超过5,600人死亡。确诊病例数为11,793例,但官员们认为,由于漏报和内乱,真实数字更高。世界卫生组织认为这是有记录以来最严重的 暴发 疫情,虽然刚果民主共和国以外地区尚未确认持续存在 暴发 疫情,但国际传播的风险仍然存在。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 世界卫生组织正在进行基因测序,并已在邻国启动健康检查。然而,暴发 却受到内战和大雨的阻碍,延误了对被困在医院产房的世卫组织工作人员的救援工作。牛津大学和印度血清研究所的实验性 疫苗 正在刚果民主共和国进行试验。

This month marked a grim milestone, with more than 5,000 deaths in the in the DRC since the outbreak began. Reports also emerged of the first confirmed case of a UK national infected with the disease, who returned to the UK for treatment at the Royal Free Hospital. Against this backdrop, two Imperial experts recently shared their insights on how the Ebola outbreak is evolving, the challenges facing responders and affected communities, and what may come next. Here’s what we learned. How big is the current Ebola outbreak? The outbreak is larger than we thought and will last well into next year. Professor Neil Ferguson, is among those leading rapid response modelling efforts. His team is currently working closely with local and international partners on: real time modelling of the outbreak, scenario modelling of vaccine deployment, and health economic analyses. Their initial analysis of the epidemic (up to June) recently published in the journal Science. “One of the major challenges at the moment is we think we're probably only detecting about half of cases which are occurring,” said Professor Ferguson, Director of the Jameel Institute for Disease and Emergency Analytics, and Director of the School of Public Health at Imperial. He explained about two-thirds of deaths from the outbreak are happening in the community, and many of these people may not come forward for healthcare. “The priority at the moment is improving detection of cases,” he adds. Professor Ferguson warns that the DRC outbreak is already comparable in scale to the 2014-15 West Africa epidemic and could ultimately become the largest Ebola outbreak on record. Based on current trends, transmission may still be occurring a year from now. But there are significant challenges in tracking the outbreak, including the sheer size and remoteness of affected regions and the inherent logistical challenges. “To put it into context, the Ituri and North Kivu provinces – the worst affected – are both the size of small European countries,” explained Professor Ferguson. “These are huge areas with limited infrastructure, a very challenging security environment, they are very poor areas and because of their history, there’s very low community trust in authorities, in government and even in health authorities.” The outbreak originated in the Eastern DRC, which is experiencing an epidemic on top of existing humanitarian and health crises (Credit: Shutterstock / slyellow). Why has the DRC been so badly affected? Conflict, poor health coverage, and endemic disease have all worsened the situation. The Eastern DRC, where the outbreak originated, has seen decades of armed conflict, insecurity and the displacement of hundreds of thousands of people, and regular outbreaks of cholera, measles and malaria have also taken a heavy toll. This combination has resulted in an epidemic occurring on top of existing humanitarian and health crises, explains Dr Aula Abbara, from Imperial’s Department of Infectious Disease. “This is all occurring in a time of severe funding cuts...and it's estimated more than 14 million people in the DRC are already in need of humanitarian assistance, many of whom live in the affected areas,” said Dr Abbara, an Honorary Clinical Associate Professor at Imperial, as well as a Consultant in Infectious Diseases at Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust and an advisor to Médecins Sans Frontières. “I was in North Kivu in June of this year,” she adds, “I'm an experienced humanitarian and I was struck by the degree of severe malnutrition and the multiple co-existing outbreaks in areas where we’re also preparing and responding to this Ebola virus disease outbreak.” What are the challenges with the Bundibugyo virus? Ebola isn’t always haemorrhagic (bleeding and bruising) so can be difficult to diagnose early on. “As a healthcare worker, it's very difficult to differentiate between BVD [Bundibugyo Viral Disease] and other infections often seen in these areas – whether it's malaria, typhoid or others – because the initial symptoms are non-specific,” Dr Abbara explained. “It's a fever, its’ fatigue, it's joint pains, it's diarrhoea, it's vomiting and so it could be mistaken for many other diseases in the early phases.” In addition, suitable treatments and medical resources are in short supply, she explains: “BVD was last seen in Uganda in 2007, and in the DRC in 2012, and unfortunately what that means is all the recent licensed Ebola vaccines and monoclonal antibodies are targeting the Zaire strain rather than the Bundibugyo strain that we're dealing with at the moment.” What are the challenges facing healthcare workers? Beyond the direct risk of infection, healthcare workers risk heat exhaustion from equipment, and additional strain on struggling services. “Wearing full PPE limits the time that a healthcare worker can be in a facility down to about 45 minutes, perhaps 60 minutes,” explained Dr Abbara. “These are very tropical areas where the outbreak’s occurring and that can lead to heat exhaustion, dehydration, and manual dexterity becomes very difficult because you're wearing two gloves. You're also wearing goggles. It becomes very cumbersome to work in these settings. And it means that there's less time for patients.” She highlighted how typical clinical tasks, such as changing IV lines and adjusting fluids, become more difficult, which can have a significant impact, especially on children. Resources are also sparse, meaning the majority of patients often won’t get access to ‘best supportive care’ – stabilising vitals, relieving pain, and enabling them to fight the infection. But the impact of the outbreak includes the indirect costs on a health system that was already under severe strain. As Dr Abbara highlights: “the impacts on children, particularly young children of both BVD and other diseases are severe and can lead to a worse illness and higher mortality; others who are vulnerable are also pregnant women who may also experience interrupted maternity care due to the outbreak.” Among the challenges are trust and misinformation, which can discourage people from seeking care, particularly when communities see substantial resources directed towards Ebola while other longstanding health threats continue to cause suffering. “Fear is keeping people away from healthcare,” explains Dr Abbara, “so indirect deaths, as often in these situations, is substantial.” How soon could we get new vaccines and treatments? While current treatment options may be limited, trials are underway which could help to turn the tide. “Clinical trials have started recently testing the existing Ervebo Ebola vaccine, but also potentially two candidate vaccines being developed,” explained Professor Ferguson, referencing candidates from the University of Oxford and an RNA vaccine from Moderna. “Those trials should read out early next year, and allow rollout of vaccination probably from late February, early March onwards,” he added. “In addition, there are clinical trials and treatments underway which probably should read out faster.” Dr Abbara added that different therapeutics are being assessed, including the antiviral Remdesivir (which became a central treatment during the COVID-19 pandemic) as well as an experimental pan-Ebolavirus antibody (MBP134) which could target multiple strains. Other teams are trialling the oral antiviral Obeldesivir to reduce the risk of infection among those who have been exposed to the virus (post-exposure prophylaxis). But challenges remain, including ensuring the right groups are included in trials. “Often children and pregnant women are excluded [from trials]. But of course, they're among those at highest risk of a poor outcome should they be exposed to an ebolavirus,” explains Dr Abbara. “Additionally, in terms of the availability of sufficient doses of these therapeutics, they’re not necessarily available to meet the need that there is in this current outbreak.” Both Imperial experts stressed that controlling the outbreak will depend not only on medical interventions, but also on building trust with affected communities and supporting local healthcare workers. Professor Ferguson concluded: “Clearly, both vaccines and effective treatments would aid the response, but neither is a panacea.” Dr Abbara added: “What we need is not only careful surveillance, medical care and diagnostics – all essential in an outbreak, but we must also work to build trust with the communities affected, reduce stigma and work very closely with the local responders to support healthcare access and trust in the services offered. Without these, people will be too afraid to access services, and we know that late presentation can contribute to poorer outcomes.” - The comments were made at an Imperial media briefing on the outbreak. Imperial College London is at the frontier of rapid response modelling, real-time tracking, and epidemiological analysis for global disease outbreaks. Our infectious disease experts apply cutting-edge science to address the unmet clinical needs for infectious disease control on a global scale. We also recently created a Biosecurity Network of Excellence to tackle the growing threats to human, animal and plant health. analysis.brief_en: A rare form of Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus has infected over 11,000 people and caused more than 5,000 deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) since May 2026. The outbreak, which originated in the Eastern DRC, is on track to become the largest in recorded history, with transmission expected to continue well into next year. Imperial College London experts, including Professor Neil Ferguson and Dr Aula Abbara, have highlighted the challenges in detecting cases, as many deaths occur in the community without seeking healthcare. The Bundibugyo virus is not targeted by recent vaccines and monoclonal antibodies, which focus on the Zaire strain. Additionally, healthcare workers face significant risks, including heat exhaustion from wearing full personal protective equipment (PPE) for limited periods. The outbreak is occurring in a region already suffering from conflict, poor health coverage, and endemic diseases, exacerbating the crisis. Efforts are ongoing to model the outbreak and improve detection, but the situation remains complex and challenging.

The outbreak, which originated in the Eastern DRC, is on track to become the largest in recorded history, with transmission expected to continue well into next year. Imperial College London experts, including Professor Neil Ferguson and Dr Aula Abbara, have highlighted the challenges in detecting cases, as many deaths occur in the community without seeking healthcare. The Bundibugyo virus is not targeted by recent vaccines and monoclonal antibodies, which focus on the Zaire strain. Additionally, healthcare workers face significant risks, including heat exhaustion from wearing full personal protective equipment (PPE) for limited periods. The outbreak is occurring in a region already suffering from conflict, poor health coverage, and endemic diseases, exacerbating the crisis. Efforts are ongoing to model the outbreak and improve detection, but the situation remains complex and challenging.
news.content_zh: 自 2026 年 5 月以来,由本迪布焦病毒引起的一种罕见埃博拉病毒已在刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 感染了 11,000 多人,并导致 5,000 多人死亡。起源于刚果民主共和国东部的 暴发 有望成为有记录以来最大规模的埃博拉疫情,传播 预计将持续到明年。伦敦帝国理工学院的专家,包括尼尔·弗格森教授和奥拉·阿巴拉博士,强调了发现病例的挑战,因为许多死亡发生在社区中而没有寻求医疗保健。本迪布焦病毒不是最近的 疫苗 和单克隆抗体的目标,这些抗体主要针对扎伊尔病毒株。此外,医护人员还面临着重大风险,包括在有限时间内穿戴全套个人防护装备 (PPE) 导致的热衰竭。暴发 事件发生在一个已经饱受冲突、医疗保健覆盖范围薄弱和地方病困扰的地区,加剧了危机。我们正在努力对 暴发 进行建模并改进检测,但情况仍然复杂且具有挑战性。

Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search Support Menu Uganda, South Sudan intensify efforts to keep Ebola out amid burgeoning DR Congo outbreak News brief November 20, 2026 Mary Van Beusekom, MS Topics Ebola Share DFID-UK Department for International Development / Flickr cc Amid the growing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), neighboring Uganda and South Sudan have tightened public-health measures and increased preparedness, and the head of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, says clinical trials of three Bundibugyo Ebola vaccines could lead to a breakthrough in the coming months if security problems can be overcome. The epidemic toll now includes 11,645 infections, including 5,683 deaths, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. This is the 17th DRC Ebola outbreak but its fast-growing and largest. It took only 40 days after the crisis was declared in mid-May to surpass 1,000 confirmed cases, compared with the 235 days for the country’s 2018 Ebola outbreak. Reducing security concerns could speed vaccine development In response to the rising number of cases and concerns about entry through unofficial border-crossing points, Uganda has restricted cross-border travel and public gatherings in 34 high-risk districts bordering the DRC. The country has forbidden concerts, festivals, and political rallies not cleared by the Ministry of Health, required a 21-day quarantine or monitored self-isolation for Ugandan travelers returning from the DRC, intensified passenger screening at airports, strengthened monitoring at hotels and schools, restricted the movement of humanitarian workers, and limited the cross-border transport of bodies. In addition, schools, hospitals, transportation terminals, churches, and other public facilities must provide handwashing stations and adhere to infection prevention and control mandates. Radio stations operating in the affected districts also must air Ebola-prevention programming for at least two hours each month. Uganda declared its outbreak over in late August. South Sudan, which has reported no Ebola infections, has also increased preparedness efforts. Four national self-assessments using a World Health Organization tool that reviews the quality of emergency readiness showed an increase in score from 29% in May to 73% in October. In the meantime, clinical trials of three vaccines targeting the Bundibugyo virus in the DRC could produce a breakthrough if security problems are resolved, Emanuele Capobianco, MD, MPH, Gavi director of global health security, told Semafor. Currently, there are no available vaccines or treatments for Bundibugyo. US flu activity continues to climb News brief November 20, 2026 Chris Dall, MA Topics Influenza, General COVID-19 Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) Tero Vesalainen / iStock The share of Americans seeking healthcare for flulike symptoms continues to rise amid an early flu season. The proportion of outpatients for influenza-like-illness (ILI) for the week ending November 14 was 3.8%, up from 3.2% the previous week and above the national baseline of 2.9% for the second consecutive week, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said today in its weekly FluView update. ILI activity increased in all regions of the country except for the Northeast, and in all age-groups, compared with the previous week. While test positivity remained flat at 11.8%, the influenza-associated hospital admission rate rose to 3.5 per 100,000 population, with the highest hospitalization rate seen in adults age 65 and over, followed by the 0 to 4 and 50 to 64-year age groups. The CDC also reported two more flu-related deaths in children, bringing the season total to seven, and a pediatric death from the 2025-26 flu season, bring that season’s total to 204 deaths. Of the viruses reported by public health laboratories, 99% have been influenza A. The CDC estimates there have been 3.7 million flu cases, 50,000 hospitalizations, and 2,800 deaths so far this season. But the agency is classifying the severity of flu activity as low across all age-groups at this point. “Many surveillance indicators are higher than typically observed at this time of year, but an earlier increase in activity does not necessarily lead to a higher seasonal peak or greater severity overall,” the CDC said, adding that it’s too early to know what viruses might predominate or whether there might be impacts on flu vaccine effectiveness. COVID, RSV at low levels In other respiratory illness updates, the CDC said both COVID-19 activity and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) activity are low nationally, but added that RSV emergency department visits are climbing in children younger than 5 years. The agency also noted that levels of rhinovirus/enterovirus are elevated but decreasing in most regions of the country, while respiratory adenovirus is elevated but stable. Both trends are typical for this time of year. Almost half of TikTok videos on RSV prevention offer inaccurate info, paper notes News brief November 20, 2026 Meghan Holohan Topics Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) skyNext / iStock Many people rely on social media to learn more about health conditions and trends. A study published in Vaccine this week that examined TikTok videos about respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) prevention—including the maternal vaccine (Abrysvo) and the long-acting antibody nirsevimab (Beyfortus) for infants—finds that only 47% present high-quality information. “Health professionals made half of all videos and most evidence-consistent content, while parents and caregivers made a larger share of mixed-or-uncertain content,” wrote the authors, from Rutgers New Jersey Medical School. Health professionals created highest-quality content The researchers watched 169 TikToks about RSV immunization using keywords such as RSV vaccine, RSV jab, or RSV prophylaxis. The videos were posted from July 17, 2023, to November 14, 2025, following the US Food and Drug Administration’s approval of nirsevimab. Using the Global Quality Scale (GQS), the scientists evaluated TikToks for quality of health information on a scale from one to five, with one representing low-quality information. Anything higher than a four is considered high-quality. The median GQS score was three, and 79 TikToks fell into the high-quality category. Healthcare professionals created most RSV-prevention TikToks (50.3%), with parents and caregivers next (37.9%), followed distantly by influencers (4.7%), social-media creators of unclear affiliation (4.1%), clinics (1.8%), and scientists and researchers (1.2%). Health professionals made half of all videos and most evidence-consistent content, while parents and caregivers made a larger share of mixed-or-uncertain content. Who created the video mattered, with healthcare professionals producing higher-quality TikToks than parents and caregivers. TikToks that offered mixed or uncertain content made up about 20% of the videos and were six times more common than misinformation (3%). RSV TikTok content “was mostly evidence-consistent and produced by clinicians, yet nearly one fifth was mixed or uncertain,” the authors said. “Given the complexity of maternal RSV vaccination and infant nirsevimab recommendations, clinicians should expect that families encounter mixed or uncertain information online and should direct them to evidence-based resources.” Quick takes: Human avian flu in Oregon, H5N9 in Japanese poultry, shorter TB treatment, polio in 3 nations News brief November 20, 2026 Mary Van Beusekom, MS Topics Avian Influenza (Bird Flu) Tuberculosis Polio Oregon health officials yesterday announced the state’s first human case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) of the year related to an outbreak at a Morrow County dairy farm. The infected person was treated with the antiviral drug oseltamivir (Tamiflu) and didn’t require hospitalization. No other details were released. In a news release, Melissa Sutton, MD, medical director for respiratory viral pathogens at the Oregon Health Authority, said the case isn’t cause for alarm. “Rather, it is evidence that the surveillance and response system we have in place is working,” she said. “Our goal is to ensure that all symptomatic farm workers receive prompt testing and treatment to prevent severe disease.” This week, Japanese authorities confirmed that the country’s first two poultry HPAI infections this year were caused by the H5N9 strain, the country’s first detection of this formerly rare subtype. The Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries said that one case each was reported in Kyoto and Chiba prefectures. A new study from Medicins Sans Frontieres (MSF) supports implementation of a shorter (four-month) treatment for children diagnosed as having non-severe, drug-susceptible tuberculosis (TB) in primary care settings. The research, conducted among 214 children in Uganda and the Philippines, found that 74% of infected children overall and up to 89% of those seen in primary care are eligible for the World Health Organization–recommended treatment. Treatment outcomes were “highly positive,” with 95% successfully completing the regimen. Implementation is feasible and uses the same drugs but substantially reduces the burden on children and their caregivers, study principal investigator Valentina Carnimeo, MPH, said in an MSF news release. “Fewer months of treatment means fewer clinic visits, less disruption to family life, lower costs for caregivers and health systems, and fewer days exposed to potential adverse effects,” she said. The Global Polio Eradication Initiative reported nine polio cases from three countries this week. Chad documented four circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) cases, while Nigeria noted two circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 3 (cVDPV3) cases, and Syria logged three circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 1 (cVDPV1) infections.
