Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search Support Menu Uganda, South Sudan intensify efforts to keep Ebola out amid burgeoning DR Congo outbreak News brief November 20, 2026 Mary Van Beusekom, MS Topics Ebola Share DFID-UK Department for International Development / Flickr cc Amid the growing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), neighboring Uganda and South Sudan have tightened public-health measures and increased preparedness, and the head of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, says clinical trials of three Bundibugyo Ebola vaccines could lead to a breakthrough in the coming months if security problems can be overcome. The epidemic toll now includes 11,645 infections, including 5,683 deaths, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. This is the 17th DRC Ebola outbreak but its fast-growing and largest. It took only 40 days after the crisis was declared in mid-May to surpass 1,000 confirmed cases, compared with the 235 days for the country’s 2018 Ebola outbreak. Reducing security concerns could speed vaccine development In response to the rising number of cases and concerns about entry through unofficial border-crossing points, Uganda has restricted cross-border travel and public gatherings in 34 high-risk districts bordering the DRC. The country has forbidden concerts, festivals, and political rallies not cleared by the Ministry of Health, required a 21-day quarantine or monitored self-isolation for Ugandan travelers returning from the DRC, intensified passenger screening at airports, strengthened monitoring at hotels and schools, restricted the movement of humanitarian workers, and limited the cross-border transport of bodies. In addition, schools, hospitals, transportation terminals, churches, and other public facilities must provide handwashing stations and adhere to infection prevention and control mandates. Radio stations operating in the affected districts also must air Ebola-prevention programming for at least two hours each month. Uganda declared its outbreak over in late August. South Sudan, which has reported no Ebola infections, has also increased preparedness efforts. Four national self-assessments using a World Health Organization tool that reviews the quality of emergency readiness showed an increase in score from 29% in May to 73% in October. In the meantime, clinical trials of three vaccines targeting the Bundibugyo virus in the DRC could produce a breakthrough if security problems are resolved, Emanuele Capobianco, MD, MPH, Gavi director of global health security, told Semafor. Currently, there are no available vaccines or treatments for Bundibugyo. The proportion of outpatients for influenza-like-illness (ILI) for the week ending November 14 was 3.8%, up from 3.2% the previous week and above the national baseline of 2.9% for the second consecutive week, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said today in its weekly FluView update. ILI activity increased in all regions of the country except for the Northeast, and in all age-groups, compared with the previous week. While test positivity remained flat at 11.8%, the influenza-associated hospital admission rate rose to 3.5 per 100,000 population, with the highest hospitalization rate seen in adults age 65 and over, followed by the 0 to 4 and 50 to 64-year age groups. The CDC also reported two more flu-related deaths in children, bringing the season total to seven, and a pediatric death from the 2025-26 flu season, bring that season’s total to 204 deaths. COVID, RSV at low levels In other respiratory illness updates, the CDC said both COVID-19 activity and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) activity are low nationally, but added that RSV emergency department visits are climbing in children younger than 5 years. Almost half of TikTok videos on RSV prevention offer inaccurate info, paper notes News brief November 20, 2026 Meghan Holohan Topics Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) skyNext / iStock Many people rely on social media to learn more about health conditions and trends. A study published in Vaccine this week that examined TikTok videos about respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) prevention—including the maternal vaccine (Abrysvo) and the long-acting antibody nirsevimab (Beyfortus) for infants—finds that only 47% present high-quality information. “Health professionals made half of all videos and most evidence-consistent content, while parents and caregivers made a larger share of mixed-or-uncertain content,” wrote the authors, from Rutgers New Jersey Medical School. Health professionals created highest-quality content The researchers watched 169 TikToks about RSV immunization using keywords such as RSV vaccine, RSV jab, or RSV prophylaxis. The videos were posted from July 17, 2023, to November 14, 2025, following the US Food and Drug Administration’s approval of nirsevimab. Using the Global Quality Scale (GQS), the scientists evaluated TikToks for quality of health information on a scale from one to five, with one representing low-quality information. Anything higher than a four is considered high-quality. The median GQS score was three, and 79 TikToks fell into the high-quality category. Healthcare professionals created most RSV-prevention TikToks (50.3%), with parents and caregivers next (37.9%), followed distantly by influencers (4.7%), social-media creators of unclear affiliation (4.1%), clinics (1.8%), and scientists and researchers (1.2%). Health professionals made half of all videos and most evidence-consistent content, while parents and caregivers made a larger share of mixed-or-uncertain content. Who created the video mattered, with healthcare professionals producing higher-quality TikToks than parents and caregivers. TikToks that offered mixed or uncertain content made up about 20% of the videos and were six times more common than misinformation (3%). RSV TikTok content “was mostly evidence-consistent and produced by clinicians, yet nearly one fifth was mixed or uncertain,” the authors said. “Given the complexity of maternal RSV vaccination and infant nirsevimab recommendations, clinicians should expect that families encounter mixed or uncertain information online and should direct them to evidence-based resources.” Quick takes: Human avian flu in Oregon, H5N9 in Japanese poultry, shorter TB treatment, polio in 3 nations News brief November 20, 2026 Mary Van Beusekom, MS Topics Avian Influenza (Bird Flu) Tuberculosis Polio Oregon health officials yesterday announced the state’s first human case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) of the year related to an outbreak at a Morrow County dairy farm. A new study from Medicins Sans Frontieres (MSF) supports implementation of a shorter (four-month) treatment for children diagnosed as having non-severe, drug-susceptible tuberculosis (TB) in primary care settings. The research, conducted among 214 children in Uganda and the Philippines, found that 74% of infected children overall and up to 89% of those seen in primary care are eligible for the World Health Organization–recommended treatment. Treatment outcomes were “highly positive,” with 95% successfully completing the regimen. Implementation is feasible and uses the same drugs but substantially reduces the burden on children and their caregivers, study principal investigator Valentina Carnimeo, MPH, said in an MSF news release. “Fewer months of treatment means fewer clinic visits, less disruption to family life, lower costs for caregivers and health systems, and fewer days exposed to potential adverse effects,” she said. Since the Ebola outbreak, almost 5,400 deaths have been reported. Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Red Cross volunteers bury a victim of Ebola in Bunia, DRC. Since the Ebola outbreak, almost 5,400 deaths have been reported. Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty Images Ebola killed 46 members of one man’s family. Now he is fighting to save the rest Six months after the Bundibugyo strain swept through eastern DR Congo, Sylvain Kabona Tibasima is still trying to warn friends and family about the dangers of the virus The day Birungi Nembe was born in a hospital in Bunia, in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, her mother, Sylvie Bongerize Tibasima, 46, was diagnosed with Ebola. Sylvie died a week later, leaving behind her husband and nine children, including her newborn daughter. But the little girl had contracted the virus shortly after birth as well. Two weeks later, in early September, her tiny body was placed in a wooden coffin, which was nailed shut and lowered into a small grave by a burial worker dressed in protective gear. Few relatives attended; the risk of infection was just too high. Six months into the deadly outbreak caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, more than 11,000 cases have been confirmed in DR Congo, with nearly 5,400 deaths reported, although aid groups estimate that actual figures may be much higher. Children account for more than a third of the deaths, according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. Several cases have also been confirmed in Kenya and Nigeria. View image in fullscreen The body of a woman who died of Ebola is taken away by Red Cross volunteers in Bunia. Photograph: Michel Lunanga/Getty The Bundibugyo virus has a reported fatality rate of almost 50%, and there is no specific treatment or approved vaccine yet, though clinical trials are continuing, according to the World Health Organization. Bunia, in the country’s eastern Ituri province, has been one of the outbreak’s centres, and Sylvie’s family has suffered an extraordinary toll: 46 relatives have died of the virus in the past months. Since the start of the epidemic, her younger brother, Sylvain Kabona Tibasima, 44, has made it his mission to educate – and warn – his relatives about the dangers of Ebola, and to keep his own family safe, including his six children. View image in fullscreen Sylvain Kabona Tibasima has received extensive training on prevention measures “It’s been incredibly difficult,” he tells the Guardian. “When Ebola began spreading, many people in this town and in my extended family believed it was sorcery. “When someone fell ill, relatives would visit them in hospital or at home. And when people died, it was customary for family members to touch the body before burial,” he says. “That’s exactly how the virus continued to spread.” Tibasima, who works as a driver for the German aid organisation Welthungerhilfe and has received extensive training on prevention measures, says he and his immediate family have taken strict precautions to protect themselves. They avoid funerals, weddings and family gatherings, keep their distance from others, wash their hands frequently and use disinfectant when outside. All of them have stayed healthy. “I keep warning my relatives about the dangers, explaining how Ebola spreads and detailing the precautions they need to take. I keep telling them we need to protect ourselves,” he says. On his phone, he holds up a photograph of his sister Sylvie; she is sitting outside on a plastic chair in a bright blue dress. It is a precious image now. He keeps scrolling. There are pictures of men and women in dresses and suits, young and old; students posing outside their school; a man standing beneath the tall trees of a nearby forest; another crouching beside his motorbike. Finally, there is a closeup of little Birungi moments after her birth: she is wrapped in a white blanket, eyes closed, sleeping peacefully. skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Sylvie Bongerize Tibasima, who died shortly after giving birth to her ninth child Tibasima has been sharing these photographs on his social media too, accompanied with crying and sad-faced emojis and messages about how much he misses each one of them. They are his brothers and sisters, aunts and uncles, cousins and other relatives who have left children orphaned. “For my children, the situation is especially stressful. They used to play outside with their friends and cousins. Now they spend most of their time indoors, hearing about their friends and cousins dying. It’s very scary,” he says. In Bunia, schools remain open, markets are busy with traders and labourers who depend on the daily income they earn there, and conflict continues to drive displacement across an already impoverished region. More than 100 armed groups operate across the eastern DR Congo, many of them in Ituri, fuelling overlapping conflicts, fighting between different ethnic groups and repeated cycles of violence. The provincial capital, Bunia, is home to more than one million displaced people, many of them living in overcrowded camps on the outskirts of the sprawling city, according to the International Organization for Migration. View image in fullscreen The crowded market in Bunia remains open despite the epidemic. The city is now home to more than a million displaced people. Photograph: Michel Lunanga/Getty Images ‘Behind every case, a person’: the man leading DRC’s Ebola fight on the human cost hidden behind the numbers Read more “Displacement, insecurity and distrust of authorities are all major obstacles to containing Ebola, as they complicate diagnosis and contact tracing,” says Pascal Cishibanji Cabwine, Welthungerhilfe’s Ebola coordinator and Tibasima’s colleague, adding that “communities have experienced years of violence and neglect, and many are now suspicious of outsiders, including government actors and international aid organisations”. More than 80 attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres have been documented since the start of the outbreak in May, putting medical staff at risk and disrupting efforts to trace contacts and contain the virus. Between 400 and 500 new cases continue to be reported each week. There are, however, some signs of hope. New infections have begun to decline in some areas, including in Bunia, although the outbreak remains far from under control. One of Tibasima’s family’s most frightening moments came a few months ago, when his daughter Malaika, 18, fell ill with symptoms that could indicate Ebola. View image in fullscreen More than 1m displaced people live in Bunia, many in camps on the city’s outskirts. Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/Getty Images “I immediately took her to the Ebola treatment centre,” he says. The rest of the family isolated at home while Malaika was tested and kept in isolation at the centre. Tibasima pulls up a photograph of his daughter. She is tall and looks confidently into the camera. After several anxious days of waiting, the family received the news they had been hoping for: Malaika had tested negative. analysis.brief_en: The article reports on a devastating Ebola outbreak in Bunia, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, caused by the Bundibugyo strain. Sylvain Kabona Tibasima, a family member, lost his wife Sylvie Bongerize Tibasima and their newborn daughter Birungi Nembe to the virus. The outbreak has claimed 46 lives in his family, with over 11,000 confirmed cases and nearly 5,400 deaths in DR Congo. The Bundibugyo virus has a high fatality rate of almost 50%, and no specific treatment or vaccine is currently available. Sylvain has taken strict measures to protect his family, including avoiding social gatherings and using disinfectant. Despite these efforts, the outbreak continues to spread, with children accounting for more than a third of the deaths. The situation remains under investigation, and the World Health Organization is conducting clinical trials for potential treatments. The article highlights the emotional toll on the affected families and the challenges of containing the virus in a region already struggling with poverty and conflict.

Faex Health Announces Investigational AI Screening Capabilities for Ebola and H. pylori, Expanding Gut Health Platform to 18 Conditions PR Newswire Fri, November 20, 2026 at 2:26 PM CST 6 min read Unveiled during HITLAB's Center for AI Testing and Evidence program, the new capabilities aim to identify potential health warning signs through smartphone images of stool, without laboratory testing for the initial assessment NEW YORK, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Faex Health, a digital health company that has developed AI-powered tools to help people better understand and track digestive wellness, announced the addition of Ebola virus disease and Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) to its investigational pre-screening platform, expanding its internally validated panel to 18 gastrointestinal and related health conditions. The announcement was made by Faex Health Co-Founder and CEO Landon Nattrass during a virtual presentation hosted by HITLAB's Center for AI Testing and Evidence (CAITE). Faex Health, a digital health company that has developed AI-powered tools to help people better understand and track digestive wellness, has been selected as a 2026 Top Innovator at the New York Venture Summit, taking place at the Javits Center in New York City through Nov. 19. The two new indications represent a significant expansion of Faex Health's research into how artificial intelligence and computer vision can identify potential health warning signs through photographs of human stool. Using a standard smartphone camera, the platform analyzes visual characteristics, including color, consistency, texture, blood, mucus, and other anomalies, to generate preliminary health indicators that may warrant further medical evaluation. While H. pylori and Ebola present dramatically different public health challenges, both underscore the potential value of accessible, noninvasive health monitoring, particularly in communities where traditional diagnostic infrastructure may be limited or difficult to access. "From one of the world's most widespread bacterial infections to one of its most dangerous viral diseases, H. pylori and Ebola illustrate the extraordinary range of public health challenges Faex Health is working to address," Nattrass said. "By expanding our investigational platform to include both conditions, we are exploring how technology people already carry in their pockets could help bridge gaps in health monitoring, particularly where access to traditional testing is limited." Addressing Two Distinct Global Health Challenges H. pylori, a bacterial infection affecting approximately half of the world's population, is a major cause of peptic ulcer disease and an established risk factor for gastric cancer. Many infected individuals experience no symptoms, making identification and treatment particularly challenging. Conventional testing typically requires a urea breath test, stool antigen test, or endoscopic biopsy. Faex Health's newly announced H. pylori indication is designed to explore whether AI analysis of stool images can provide an accessible preliminary signal that encourages appropriate follow-up testing and medical evaluation. Ebola virus disease, by contrast, is a rare but potentially fatal infectious disease that can cause severe gastrointestinal symptoms, including diarrhea and significant fluid loss. Confirmatory diagnosis requires specialized laboratory testing, typically using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). Story Continues Faex Health is investigating whether visual patterns in stool could contribute to preliminary triage assessments in outbreak environments, particularly where laboratory resources are limited or delays in testing may complicate public health response. The technology is not intended to diagnose Ebola or replace established laboratory testing, infection-control procedures or clinical assessment. Both new indications have undergone internal validation using Faex Health's proprietary datasets. Neither has entered clinical trials, and neither has received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) clearance or approval. Expanding AI-Powered Monitoring Across 18 Health Conditions With the addition of Ebola and H. pylori, Faex Health's investigational platform now encompasses 18 conditions across five clinical categories, including infectious diseases; colorectal and gastrointestinal bleeding conditions; chronic and inflammatory disorders; functional and anorectal conditions; and hepatic, pancreatic and microbiome-related conditions. The panel includes investigational indicators associated with colorectal cancer risk, precancerous polyps, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, irritable bowel syndrome, celiac disease, gastrointestinal bleeding, and other digestive health concerns. Unlike traditional stool testing methods that capture information at a single point in time, Faex Health is designed to support ongoing monitoring through repeated smartphone images. Its computer vision technology evaluates stool characteristics consistently over time, creating the potential to identify changes and patterns that may otherwise go unrecorded. The platform also provides Bristol Stool Form Scale classifications and evaluates seven categories of visual anomalies. "Your gut produces information about your health every day, yet most of that information is never captured or evaluated," Nattrass added. "Our vision is to make monitoring those changes as routine as checking your heart rate or tracking your sleep. Rather than relying exclusively on isolated tests, we believe longitudinal data could eventually provide healthcare professionals and individuals with a more complete picture of digestive health." Advancing Clinical Research and Commercial Deployment Faex Health's broader research program includes the ongoing FECAL-AI clinical trial at Hospital Dr. Sótero del Río in Chile, where investigators are evaluating the platform's image-derived signals in colorectal cancer screening against conventional fecal immunochemical testing (FIT). The company is also exploring the design of a larger-scale colorectal cancer screening study in the United Kingdom involving the National Health Service (NHS) and National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR). That proposed program remains in the planning stage and has not received protocol approval. Commercially, Faex Health reports four signed agreements representing approximately 150,000 covered lives, with its first 50,000 covered lives active as of November 2026. Beyond its current 18-condition investigational panel, Faex Health is conducting exploratory research into stool-visible indicators associated with more than 100 additional health conditions. Nattrass will further discuss the company's research, clinical development and vision for AI-powered health monitoring at the HITLAB Innovators Summit on Dec. 3 at the Microsoft Technology Center in Times Square, New York City. For more information or to schedule an interview, contact Shawna Seldon at shawna@themaverickpr.com or +1 917-971-7852. About Faex Health Faex Health is a health technology company that has developed AI-powered solutions for preventive gastrointestinal health monitoring. Using computer vision, machine learning, and smartphone-based image analysis, the Faex platform helps users capture digestive health information, monitor patterns over time, and access personalized educational wellness insights. The company has developed solutions designed to support individuals, healthcare providers, health plans, employers, and population health organizations. Faex Health's investigational clinical applications are intended to complement established medical screening and diagnostic pathways, not replace them. For more information, visit FaexHealth.com. Download the Faex Health app on Apple Store for iOS and Google Play for Android. Continue the conversation on LinkedIn, Facebook, TikTok, X, Reddit, and Instagram. Regulatory and Clinical Research Disclosure: Faex Health is investigational and has not received FDA clearance or approval. Its outputs are preliminary pre-screening indicators intended for health awareness and professional review, not medical diagnoses. All 18 indications have undergone internal validation, but these findings have not been independently replicated or peer reviewed as a complete panel. Clinical trials have not begun for the Ebola or H. pylori indications. The platform is not a substitute for laboratory testing, established screening protocols or professional medical evaluation. Faex Health Announces Investigational AI Screening Capabilities for Ebola and H. pylori, Expanding Gut Health Platform to 18 Conditions PR Newswire Fri, November 20, 2026 at 2:26 PM CST 6 min read Unveiled during HITLAB's Center for AI Testing and Evidence program, the new capabilities aim to identify potential health warning signs through smartphone images of stool, without laboratory testing for the initial assessment NEW YORK, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Faex Health, a digital health company that has developed AI-powered tools to help people better understand and track digestive wellness, announced the addition of Ebola virus disease and Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) to its investigational pre-screening platform, expanding its internally validated panel to 18 gastrointestinal and related health conditions. The announcement was made by Faex Health Co-Founder and CEO Landon Nattrass during a virtual presentation hosted by HITLAB's Center for AI Testing and Evidence (CAITE). Faex Health, a digital health company that has developed AI-powered tools to help people better understand and track digestive wellness, has been selected as a 2026 Top Innovator at the New York Venture Summit, taking place at the Javits Center in New York City through Nov. 19. The two new indications represent a significant expansion of Faex Health's research into how artificial intelligence and computer vision can identify potential health warning signs through photographs of human stool. Using a standard smartphone camera, the platform analyzes visual characteristics, including color, consistency, texture, blood, mucus, and other anomalies, to generate preliminary health indicators that may warrant further medical evaluation. While H. pylori and Ebola present dramatically different public health challenges, both underscore the potential value of accessible, noninvasive health monitoring, particularly in communities where traditional diagnostic infrastructure may be limited or difficult to access. "From one of the world's most widespread bacterial infections to one of its most dangerous viral diseases, H. pylori and Ebola illustrate the extraordinary range of public health challenges Faex Health is working to address," Nattrass said. "By expanding our investigational platform to include both conditions, we are exploring how technology people already carry in their pockets could help bridge gaps in health monitoring, particularly where access to traditional testing is limited." Addressing Two Distinct Global Health Challenges H. pylori, a bacterial infection affecting approximately half of the world's population, is a major cause of peptic ulcer disease and an established risk factor for gastric cancer. Many infected individuals experience no symptoms, making identification and treatment particularly challenging. Conventional testing typically requires a urea breath test, stool antigen test, or endoscopic biopsy. Faex Health's newly announced H. pylori indication is designed to explore whether AI analysis of stool images can provide an accessible preliminary signal that encourages appropriate follow-up testing and medical evaluation. Ebola virus disease, by contrast, is a rare but potentially fatal infectious disease that can cause severe gastrointestinal symptoms, including diarrhea and significant fluid loss. Confirmatory diagnosis requires specialized laboratory testing, typically using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). Story Continues Faex Health is investigating whether visual patterns in stool could contribute to preliminary triage assessments in outbreak environments, particularly where laboratory resources are limited or delays in testing may complicate public health response. The technology is not intended to diagnose Ebola or replace established laboratory testing, infection-control procedures or clinical assessment. Both new indications have undergone internal validation using Faex Health's proprietary datasets. Neither has entered clinical trials, and neither has received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) clearance or approval. Expanding AI-Powered Monitoring Across 18 Health Conditions With the addition of Ebola and H. pylori, Faex Health's investigational platform now encompasses 18 conditions across five clinical categories, including infectious diseases; colorectal and gastrointestinal bleeding conditions; chronic and inflammatory disorders; functional and anorectal conditions; and hepatic, pancreatic and microbiome-related conditions. The panel includes investigational indicators associated with colorectal cancer risk, precancerous polyps, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, irritable bowel syndrome, celiac disease, gastrointestinal bleeding, and other digestive health concerns. Unlike traditional stool testing methods that capture information at a single point in time, Faex Health is designed to support ongoing monitoring through repeated smartphone images. Its computer vision technology evaluates stool characteristics consistently over time, creating the potential to identify changes and patterns that may otherwise go unrecorded. The platform also provides Bristol Stool Form Scale classifications and evaluates seven categories of visual anomalies. "Your gut produces information about your health every day, yet most of that information is never captured or evaluated," Nattrass added. "Our vision is to make monitoring those changes as routine as checking your heart rate or tracking your sleep. Rather than relying exclusively on isolated tests, we believe longitudinal data could eventually provide healthcare professionals and individuals with a more complete picture of digestive health." Advancing Clinical Research and Commercial Deployment Faex Health's broader research program includes the ongoing FECAL-AI clinical trial at Hospital Dr. Sótero del Río in Chile, where investigators are evaluating the platform's image-derived signals in colorectal cancer screening against conventional fecal immunochemical testing (FIT). The company is also exploring the design of a larger-scale colorectal cancer screening study in the United Kingdom involving the National Health Service (NHS) and National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR). That proposed program remains in the planning stage and has not received protocol approval. Commercially, Faex Health reports four signed agreements representing approximately 150,000 covered lives, with its first 50,000 covered lives active as of November 2026. Beyond its current 18-condition investigational panel, Faex Health is conducting exploratory research into stool-visible indicators associated with more than 100 additional health conditions. Nattrass will further discuss the company's research, clinical development and vision for AI-powered health monitoring at the HITLAB Innovators Summit on Dec. 3 at the Microsoft Technology Center in Times Square, New York City. For more information or to schedule an interview, contact Shawna Seldon at shawna@themaverickpr.com or +1 917-971-7852. About Faex Health Faex Health is a health technology company that has developed AI-powered solutions for preventive gastrointestinal health monitoring. Using computer vision, machine learning, and smartphone-based image analysis, the Faex platform helps users capture digestive health information, monitor patterns over time, and access personalized educational wellness insights. The company has developed solutions designed to support individuals, healthcare providers, health plans, employers, and population health organizations. Faex Health's investigational clinical applications are intended to complement established medical screening and diagnostic pathways, not replace them. For more information, visit FaexHealth.com. Download the Faex Health app on Apple Store for iOS and Google Play for Android. Continue the conversation on LinkedIn, Facebook, TikTok, X, Reddit, and Instagram. Regulatory and Clinical Research Disclosure: Faex Health is investigational and has not received FDA clearance or approval. Its outputs are preliminary pre-screening indicators intended for health awareness and professional review, not medical diagnoses. All 18 indications have undergone internal validation, but these findings have not been independently replicated or peer reviewed as a complete panel. Clinical trials have not begun for the Ebola or H. pylori indications. The platform is not a substitute for laboratory testing, established screening protocols or professional medical evaluation. news.content_zh: 数字健康公司 Faex Health 于 2026 年 11 月 20 日宣布,已扩展其人工智能预筛查平台,将 埃博拉病毒病 和幽门螺杆菌纳入其中,使胃肠道及相关疾病的总数达到 18 种。Faex Health 联合创始人兼首席执行官 Landon Nattrass 在 HITLAB 人工智能测试和证据中心 (CAITE) 的虚拟演示中宣布了这一消息。该平台使用智能手机的粪便图像来分析颜色、稠度、质地、血液和粘液等视觉特征,以生成初步的健康指标。这一发展旨在通过提供易于使用的非侵入性筛查工具来应对公共卫生挑战,特别是在诊断资源有限的地区。虽然埃博拉病毒的确认性 诊断 需要专门的实验室测试,但人工智能工具旨在提供可能鼓励进一步医学评估的初始信号。这些影响凸显了利用现有技术改善 暴发 环境中的健康监测和响应的潜力。

Half of the 11,000 infected in Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) – where the outbreak was first declared – have died, while cases have been spotted in Kenya, Nigeria, Uganda and France. 5 Global spread of Ebola could be possible if the outbreak continues to grow, Africa’s WHO chief has warned Source: Reuters 5 Dr Mohamed Janabi called for the UK and other countries to help curb the outbreak Source: Alamy Advertisement A British health worker infected with the deadly illness on the ground was also evacuated back to the UK for treatment earlier this month. The rare Bundibugyo strain, which has a mortality rate of 30 to 50 per cent, is behind this outbreak – first declared in May, but officials believe it started spreading at the beginning of the year. Sign up for The US Sun newsletter Thank you! Email address Please provide a valid email. Your info will be used in accordance with our Privacy Policy You'll now receive top stories, breaking news, and more, straight to your email. The variant is spreading at double the pace of the 2014-2016 Ebola outbreak ‌in West Africa, the largest on record. A big reason for this is that there’s no vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain, but conflict, displacement, lack of access to remote areas and distrust of health workers have further fuelled spread. Read more on Ebola VIRUS ALERT Brit doctor who tested positive for Ebola arrives to UK hospital for treatment VIRAL PANIC Rapidly growing Ebola outbreak ‘poses threat worldwide’ as HALF of infected die Dr Mohamed Janabi, the World Health Organisation’s (WHO) Regional Director for Africa warned international spread of the virus is “possible” if more isn’t done to stop it. He told Metro: “The virus was ahead of us for four months. “Insecurity, population movement, and transmission in hard-to-reach areas are making it harder to break the chains of transmission. “As long as the outbreak continues to spread further, I have to say that spread [internationally] is possible.” Advertisement Most read in Health TRAGIC LOSS ‘Healthy’ wife-to-be, 30, suffered flu-like symptoms before her sudden death HORROR stunt Man, 35, dies after rectum EXPLODES doing 'silly experiment' at factory job HEALTH HAZARD Health experts warn of surge in disease dating back to the Dark Ages HOSPITAL TRAGEDY Woman, 24, 'died when she was given oxygen mask not connected to anything' 5 Dr Janabi with WHO director and incident manager Marie Roseline Belizaire (L) and WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus Source: AFP 5 The outbreak is being caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain Source: Reuters An Ebola case was detected in France in June, in a doctor who had been on a humanitarian trip to the DRC. Another patient with the deadly disease travelled to the United Arab Emirates before going on to Uganda. When asked if further transmission like this was possible, Dr Janabi said that “global risk is still low” but warned that similar “spread is possible” if the outbreak worsens. Advertisement Professor Neil Ferguson, director of the Jameel Institute for Disease and Emergency Analytics, and the School of Public Health at Imperial recently warned this Ebola outbreak is on track to become the largest on record. Based on current trends, it may still be spreading a year from now. But there are significant challenges in tracking the outbreak, including the sheer size and remoteness of affected regions. Prof Ferguson explained: “To put it into context, the Ituri and North Kivu provinces – the worst affected – are both the size of small European countries. “These are huge areas with limited infrastructure, a very challenging security environment, they are very poor areas and because of their history, there’s very low community trust in authorities, in government and even in health authorities.” Advertisement Dr Janabi claimed officials are “turning the tide” in places hit hardest at the beginning of the outbreak, with cases “falling sharply” in the city of Bunia. But he warned that health officials can’t intervene in areas affected by militia conflict. 5 Red Cross workers disinfecting Rwampara general hospital Source: Reuters How does Ebola spread and what are the symptoms? The virus is transmitted through direct contact with blood and body fluids and objects that have been contaminated by someone with Ebola. It also spreads through contact with sick or dead wild animals. It can take two to 21 days for symptoms to appear following infection – this is known as an incubation period. Ebola first appears as a high fever, intense muscle and joint pain, headaches and a sore throat. Initial symptoms are often followed by vomiting and diarrhoea, rashes on the skin, kidney and liver failure, and sometimes internal and external bleeding. People who survive the virus can suffer from arthritis as well as vision and hearing problems. Some types of Ebola can be prevented with vaccines and treated with medicines. Source: World Health Organization Meanwhile, a recent Reuters analysis of satellite imagery that examined the number of graves dug in Bunia since the conflict began suggests the true Ebola death toll may be higher than official counts suggest. Dr Janabi pleaded with the UK and other Western countries to step up support and funding for tackling the deadly disease. Advertisement He said: “They must be partners, not bystanders, in shaping the response. “Why don’t we equip countries with modern equipment for screening? Why don’t we equip them with treatment centres?” Dr Janabi remained optimistic that the virus can be contained. He said: “I strongly believe inside me we are going to put a halt in Ebola Bundibugyo. “My data shows we have discharged over 3000 cases of confirmed Ebola. Advertisement “We started with zero treatment centres and now we have over 40 in the region. “The trials with a vaccine are continuing well, and I think early next year we are going to be ready to share the outcome.” The scientist said he had met multiple UK ambassadors and representatives from other countries to discuss their response to the virus and raise the issue of vaccines. Jabs against the Bundibugyo strain are currently in development, but Dr Janabi worried the DRC would not get priority access to them. A UK Government spokesperson told Metro: “We share Dr Janabi’s determination to bring this outbreak under control. Advertisement “The UK is deeply concerned by the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and our priority is to help stop transmission, save lives and prevent wider regional spread. “The UK is providing £78.7 million to support the response, alongside technical expertise and diplomatic engagement, helping to strengthen surveillance, treatment and infection prevention and support frontline health workers and affected communities. “We are working closely with the DRC authorities, Africa CDC, WHO and other partners on the immediate response, as well as supporting efforts to develop new vaccines, treatments and diagnostics and ensure they can reach the people who need them.” Ebola has an incubation period of up to three weeks, but once symptoms start they can include fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding. But bleeding is only occurring in around 5 to 10 per cent of confirmed cases in the Bundibugyo outbreak, Yap Boum, Africa CDC’s deputy Ebola incident manager, recently told Reuters. Advertisement This makes the symptom less common than in outbreaks of the more prevalent Ebola strain, Zaire. It means the disease might be easier to confuse with other more common illnesses like malaria, which may have contributed to the late detection of the outbreak alongside early challenges with diagnosis, as the tests designed for other Ebola species do not pick up Bundibugyo. RECOMMENDED STORIES It is also making it harder to track the spread, as many people do not suspect Ebola and seek care. Around 70 per cent of patients are still dying in their communities rather than in healthcare centres. analysis.time: The outbreak was first declared in May 2026, with cases reported in Kenya, Nigeria, Uganda, and France. The publication date is 2026-11-23, and the event date is 2026-11-24.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak is primarily in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), specifically in the Ituri and North Kivu provinces. Cases have also been reported in Kenya, Nigeria, Uganda, and France.
analysis.event: An unprecedented Ebola outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain, has been reported. The World Health Organization (WHO) chief, Dr. Mohamed Janabi, warned that the outbreak could spread globally if not contained. The death toll has reached 5,500, and the outbreak is spreading at double the pace of the 2014-2016 West African outbreak.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Half of the 11,000 infected in the DRC have died, with cases detected in multiple countries. The mortality rate for the Bundibugyo strain is 30 to 50 percent. The global risk is described as low, but the WHO chief warned that spread is possible if the outbreak worsens. The outbreak is spreading rapidly in remote and conflict-affected areas.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The WHO chief called for increased support and funding from the UK and other Western countries. Efforts include contact tracing, isolation, and setting up treatment centers. However, challenges remain due to conflict, displacement, and limited infrastructure in affected regions. The outbreak is being tracked, but the true death toll may be higher than official counts.

analysis.brief_en: An unprecedented Ebola outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain, has been reported in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), with a death toll reaching 5,500. The World Health Organization (WHO) chief, Dr. Mohamed Janabi, warned that the outbreak could spread globally if not contained, citing the lack of a vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain and challenges such as conflict, displacement, and distrust of health workers. Cases have been detected in Kenya, Nigeria, Uganda, and France, with the outbreak spreading at double the pace of the 2014-2016 West African outbreak. Dr. Janabi emphasized the need for international support and funding, calling for countries to be equipped with modern screening and treatment facilities. Despite efforts to contain the outbreak, the situation remains complex due to the size and remoteness of affected regions, as well as the low community trust in authorities. The WHO remains optimistic about containing the virus, but the risk of further spread is still present.

news.content: What’s really driving the Ebola outbreak? Vaccine trials are underway—but the crisis needs far more than a medical solution, experts say By Sanidhya Sharma & Mary Randolph edited by Claire Cameron Health workers demonstrate medical procedures to the community. For Marie-Roseline Bélizaire, a typical day starts around 6 A.M. at a health center in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where she pores over freshly confirmed Ebola cases that have come in overnight. From then on, the work is nonstop: she calls dozens of provinces, visits health centers, supervises contact tracing, trains emergency workers and woos donors—as well as any number of other urgent tasks—before she falls asleep and does it all again the next day. Bélizaire, emergency director for the World Health Organization’s Regional Office for Africa, does not expect this work to let up anytime soon. She is on the front line, trying desperately to contain the current Ebola outbreak as it rages across central Africa. “Our biggest concern right now is that the outbreak is still evolving, and we’re still having a lot of people dying in the community,” she says. This Ebola outbreak was declared in the DRC in May . By November 17, it had expanded to five countries, with more than 11,600 recorded cases and more than 5,600 deaths. The disease is being driven by a distinct species of virus called Bundibugyo . After a 2014–2016 outbreak of a different Ebola-causing virus in West Africa (in which Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were the hardest-hit countries), this is the second-largest outbreak of the disease in history and the fastest-spreading ever. Sanidhya Sharma; Sources: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention ( cases and deaths ); World Health Organization ( dates ) Scientists know little about Bundibugyo and how to treat it clinically —but the public health crisis will take far more than medical measures to solve, experts say. Bundibugyo is a rare species of Ebola-causing virus. It has seen only two previous outbreaks, in 2007 and 2012. Symptoms of Bundibugyo infection, as with other cases of Ebola, include fever, diarrhea, vomiting, headaches and difficulty breathing. Because experts have seen so little of this species of virus before and because the DRC is in social and political turmoil, it’s difficult to determine the exact death rate or how the strain might be evolving. When virologists were developing vaccines for Ebola during the 2014–2016 outbreak, they did not include Bundibugyo . In primate studies, Bundibugyo appeared less lethal and did not act as fast as other strains, says Tom Geisbert, a virologist at the University of Texas Medical Branch at Galveston. Geisbert helped develop the Ervebo vaccine, which treats the Ebola virus (formerly the Zaire virus), a different species than Bundibugyo. Now, Geisbert says, Bundibugyo’s slow-to-appear symptoms mean that asymptomatic people may infect others for days before they are diagnosed themselves. “We guessed wrong,” he says of the past vaccine effort. “There just wasn’t enough effort put on Bundibugyo to be ready for that.” Research is now underway on potential Bundibugyo vaccines , including Ervebo, along with a vaccine from the University of Oxford that specifically targets Bundibugyo and an mRNA-based vaccine from Moderna. All three have been approved for a phase 2/3 trial that will test the shots on participants in the outbreak zone. Geisbert says he hopes to see a vaccine approved in the first quarter of 2027. Sanidhya Sharma; Sources: National Institute of Public Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, situation reports Nos. 178–187 (November 2026); World Health Organization ( 2014 and 2026 outbreak data ) But many of the reasons for the outbreak’s rapid growth aren’t clinical—and the crisis will not end with the arrival of a vaccine. Successful treatment for infectious disease relies on contact tracing: accurate tracking of whom a patient could have infected. Right now, about 65 percent of Ebola deaths are happening within community settings, rather than at well-equipped treatment centers. That makes it more difficult to track infected or exposed people’s movements. The DRC’s health ministry recently said that its tracing rate for known contacts had reached roughly 86 percent, but John Johnson, a vaccination and epidemic response adviser at Doctors Without Borders, says he’d be “shocked” if any of the 68 affected health zones in the country were able to track such a high proportion of the actual number of people exposed. “From what I’ve heard, pretty much everybody says contact tracing is nearly nonexistent in most of these places, and that’s why we’re having so much community death,” he says. Collecting data is difficult within extremely mobile populations affected by instability. The borders in central Africa are generally porous, and people are constantly traveling across them. The DRC is also facing severe insecurity marked by violent armed conflict across the country, which causes further displacement. Sanidhya Sharma; Sources: National Institute of Public Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, situation report No. 187 (November 18, 2026; DRC data ); European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (November 16, 2026; Uganda and Kenya data ); GRID3 ; Natural Earth ( boundaries ) When just one infected person moves, it can start a new chain of transmission—and people are moving by the thousands, says the WHO’s Bélizaire. At the same time, there are more people living in dense urban centers, making the opportunity for spread even greater, she adds. If and when responders can get a fast-acting vaccine and a handle on contact tracing—and those are big ifs, experts warn—they face communities hardened by years of insecurity and distrust, says Joanne Liu, an epidemiologist at McGill University and former international president of Doctors Without Borders. Liu visited the DRC several times during a 2018–2019 Ebola outbreak and says she often heard from communities that they had bigger problems than the virus, including malaria, pneumonia, contaminated water and violent attacks. She calls the situation there a “mille-feuille context”—so full of layers and complexity that solutions must start and end with communities themselves. “What they see is a massive mobilization of aid coming for one specific disease, when actually their challenge is all of the other infectious diseases, plus the insecurity, and nobody is paying attention,” she says. Liu worries that amid distrust and constant movement, the outbreak could spread farther to places such as the Central African Republic and South Sudan, which have little to no international public health infrastructure, making vaccination campaigns even more challenging. “It’s one thing to have a vaccine—it’s another thing that it transforms itself into a vaccination. A shot is only good once it’s in people’s arms,” she says. Great science journalism requires human expertise, time, effort and creativity. And it costs money. news.content_zh: 文章讨论了刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 正在爆发的埃博拉病毒 暴发,该病毒于 2026 年 5 月宣布,并于 2026 年 11 月 17 日扩大到五个国家。该病毒报告了 11,600 多例病例和 5,600 多人死亡,使其成为历史上第二大、传播速度最快的埃博拉病毒 暴发。暴发 是由 Bundibugyo 病毒驱动的,这是一种稀有的 埃博拉病毒 病毒,之前仅在 2007 年和 2012 年出现过两次 暴发。与早期 疫苗 开发的重点扎伊尔病毒不同,Bundibugyo 具有不同的临床特征,包括症状发作较慢,这使遏制变得复杂。世界卫生组织紧急事务主任 Marie-Rosine Bélizaire 强调了接触者追踪和社区参与的挑战,并指出 65% 的死亡发生在 治疗 中心之外。尽管进行了 疫苗 试验,包括 Ervebo 以及来自 Oxford 和 Moderna 的新选择,但专家警告说,暴发 的快速传播是由于医疗干预之外的因素造成的,例如人口流动和社会不稳定。刚果民主共和国卫生部报告接触者追踪率为 86%,但遭到无国界医生组织的质疑。暴发 仍然是一个重大的公共卫生挑战,专家强调需要基于社区的解决方案。

news.content: MENU SUBSCRIBE SUBSCRIBE Menu Item Menu Item Menu Item MENU News Sports Opinion Features Business About Local Editions ► Chatham News & Record Duplin Journal Hoke County Edition Moore County Edition Randolph Record Stanly News Journal Twin City Herald News Sports Opinion Features Business About Local Editions Chatham News & Record Duplin Journal Hoke County Edition Moore County Edition Randolph Record Stanly News Journal Twin City Herald November 25, 2026 Ebola outbreak remains out of control in Congo Six months into the response, nearly half of the 11,000 infected have died November 23, 2026 The Associated Press News Healthcare workers carry the body of a 10-month-old who died of the Ebola virus near a morgue in Bunia, Congo, on Sunday. (Dieudonne Dirole / AP Photo) BUNIA, Congo — Six months after an Ebola outbreak was declared in Congo, the disease remains out of control and efforts to contain it are faltering. More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to government data. It is the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016. Basic containment measures, including contact tracing and isolation, remain inadequate, raising doubts about authorities’ ability to halt the outbreak. Experts say there is little chance of bringing it under control within the next year. By the time the outbreak was announced in mid-May, 43 deaths had already been recorded, suggesting the virus had circulated undetected for an extended period. It has since spread to eight of the country’s 26 provinces, moving at a pace aid groups have likened to wildfire. New hotspots continue to emerge, stretching an already strained healthcare system. Community transmission remains high. According to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 80% of new cases are being detected outside health surveillance, meaning most infections have not been tracked by authorities. One-third of deaths occur at home or elsewhere in the community, where burials and other procedures are often conducted without specialist supervision, increasing the risk of transmission. Health workers have repeatedly gone on strike over pay that is months overdue, sometimes leaving patients with confirmed infections without treatment. Aid groups have also questioned how the response is being managed. Last month, the Africa CDC raised concerns about more than $700 million in Ebola aid that remains unaccounted for. “A troubling disconnect between the considerable resources mobilised for the response and what is actually reaching patients, frontline workers, and communities continues,” said the humanitarian organization Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF. Children are particularly vulnerable to Ebola, especially those with preexisting conditions such as malnutrition, experts say. Most children affected by the disease have not received specialized care, contributing to high death rates. According to UNICEF, children accounted for 35% of deaths recorded through Nov. 4. Children under 5 accounted for 21% of all deaths, and nearly 72% of infected children in that age group have died. Health workers face difficult conditions as Ebola prevention and containment measures clash with social and cultural practices. Since the outbreak began, health workers have been attacked, some fatally, adding to the dangers of working in an already volatile region. Health facilities have also come under attack. The outbreak has been concentrated in eastern Congo, particularly Ituri and North Kivu, where communities face both the epidemic and armed conflict. Fighting between government forces and hundreds of rebel groups, including the Rwanda-backed M23, had already helped create one of the world’s most severe humanitarian crises. The Allied Democratic Forces, an Islamic State-affiliated rebel group, also attacks civilians. The virus’ rapid spread has raised fears of wider transmission across Africa. Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda have confirmed cases, making this the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak on record. analysis.time: Six months into the response, nearly half of the 11,000 infected have died (N1). The outbreak was declared in mid-May (N27). The publication date is November 23, 2026 (N1).
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak has been concentrated in eastern Congo, particularly Ituri and North Kivu (N24). It has spread to eight of the country’s 26 provinces (N8).
analysis.event: An Ebola outbreak remains out of control in Congo, with nearly half of the 11,000 infected cases resulting in deaths (N3). The outbreak is described as the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks (N4).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, with nearly half of the infected dying (N3). The outbreak has spread to eight provinces, and community transmission remains high (N8, N10). It is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak (N4).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Basic containment measures, including contact tracing and isolation, remain inadequate (N5). Health workers have faced strikes over unpaid wages, leaving patients without treatment (N13). The Africa CDC has raised concerns about unaccounted aid funds (N15).

analysis.brief_en: An Ebola outbreak in Congo remains out of control, with over 11,000 cases reported and nearly half of the infected individuals succumbing to the disease. The outbreak, declared in mid-May, has spread to eight provinces, including Ituri and North Kivu, where communities face both the epidemic and armed conflict. Despite efforts, basic containment measures such as contact tracing and isolation are insufficient, and health workers have gone on strike over unpaid wages, impacting patient care. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention note that 80% of new cases are detected outside official surveillance, and community burials contribute to transmission risks. The outbreak is the deadliest in Congo’s history and could surpass the West African outbreak’s death toll. The situation highlights challenges in resource allocation and management, with over $700 million in aid remaining unaccounted for.

Facebook Twitter Print Email DR Congo: Concern for trapped Ebola workers as violence against women and girls deepens 24 November 2026 Health Staff from the World Health Organization (WHO) and Ebola responders remain trapped in a hospital in Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as heavy fighting continues in the vicinity, the UN agency said in an update on Tuesday. The health workers have been sheltering in a maternity ward since fighting began on Saturday near where the outbreak first emerged in May. “Conflict as well as torrential rain yesterday meant that we were not able to move them safely. We’re hoping to do this as soon as possible, ideally today,” WHO Spokesperson Christian Lindmeier told journalists in Geneva. He upheld that hospitals must be maintained as safe spaces during conflict. The development comes as health personnel work to contain spread of Ebola disease caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus species, with more than 11,613 confirmed cases and 5,678 deaths, according to latest WHO figures. Ituri and Nord Kivu in the volatile eastern DRC remain the most affected provinces. Rise in violence against women and girls Meanwhile, Ebola is putting immense pressure on families, and women and girls are bearing much of the burden as fear of the virus limits their movements and puts them at risk of violence and abuse. That’s according to the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) which on Tuesday released iniital findings on what is believed to be the first real-time surveillance of violence against women and adolescent girls during an active disease outbreak. The study is being carried out with SOFEPADI, a veteran Congolese women-led organization, and Washington University in the United States. Researchers have so far spoken to 1,062 women and adolescent girls across five health zones in Ituri province, the epicentre of the outbreak. They are also hearing from young people via a UNICEF digital platform called U-Report and talking to frontline workers. "This surveillance is helping us understand where risks are increasing while there’s still time to do something about it. And what we're already hearing is concerning, " said Dr. Douglas Noble, UNICEF Global Lead for Public Health Emergencies and Global Incident Manager for Ebola, speaking fresh from a visit to eastern DRC. Control, physical abuse and sexual violence Nearly six in 10 women and girls said that violence and abuse had started or increased in their lives since the Ebola outbreak began. “More than a third described someone taking more control over their lives, followed by emotional and psychological abuse. Others reported physical and sexual violence,” he said. Additionally, seven in 10 respondents live in households that have been through isolation, quarantine or contact tracing. Of them, nearly two in three reported new or increased violence which nine in 10 linked to the stress and fear caused by the outbreak. Health crisis, new threats “In Ituri, years of conflict and displacement means women and girls were already living with very high level of violence. Facebook Twitter Print Email DR Congo: Concern for trapped Ebola workers as violence against women and girls deepens 24 November 2026 Health Staff from the World Health Organization (WHO) and Ebola responders remain trapped in a hospital in Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as heavy fighting continues in the vicinity, the UN agency said in an update on Tuesday. The health workers have been sheltering in a maternity ward since fighting began on Saturday near where the outbreak first emerged in May. “Conflict as well as torrential rain yesterday meant that we were not able to move them safely. We’re hoping to do this as soon as possible, ideally today,” WHO Spokesperson Christian Lindmeier told journalists in Geneva. He upheld that hospitals must be maintained as safe spaces during conflict. The development comes as health personnel work to contain spread of Ebola disease caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus species, with more than 11,613 confirmed cases and 5,678 deaths, according to latest WHO figures. Ituri and Nord Kivu in the volatile eastern DRC remain the most affected provinces. Rise in violence against women and girls Meanwhile, Ebola is putting immense pressure on families, and women and girls are bearing much of the burden as fear of the virus limits their movements and puts them at risk of violence and abuse. That’s according to the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) which on Tuesday released iniital findings on what is believed to be the first real-time surveillance of violence against women and adolescent girls during an active disease outbreak. The study is being carried out with SOFEPADI, a veteran Congolese women-led organization, and Washington University in the United States. Researchers have so far spoken to 1,062 women and adolescent girls across five health zones in Ituri province, the epicentre of the outbreak. They are also hearing from young people via a UNICEF digital platform called U-Report and talking to frontline workers. "This surveillance is helping us understand where risks are increasing while there’s still time to do something about it. And what we're already hearing is concerning, " said Dr. Douglas Noble, UNICEF Global Lead for Public Health Emergencies and Global Incident Manager for Ebola, speaking fresh from a visit to eastern DRC. Control, physical abuse and sexual violence Nearly six in 10 women and girls said that violence and abuse had started or increased in their lives since the Ebola outbreak began. “More than a third described someone taking more control over their lives, followed by emotional and psychological abuse. Others reported physical and sexual violence,” he said. Additionally, seven in 10 respondents live in households that have been through isolation, quarantine or contact tracing. Of them, nearly two in three reported new or increased violence which nine in 10 linked to the stress and fear caused by the outbreak. Health crisis, new threats “In Ituri, years of conflict and displacement means women and girls were already living with very high level of violence. Now on top of everything else, this health crisis brings new threats of violence, stigma, fear and difficulty reaching essential services,” said Sandrine Lusamba, the SOFEPADI National Coordinator. The organization runs eight safe spaces across the province where women and girls can talk confidentially, receive psychosocial support and be referred to medical, legal and other services. She said the number of visits has risen from 1,183 between January and March to 3,584 between July and September – a threefold increase. “Some women tells us about the violence they face in their homes. Others describe the insecurity they face when they go out to find food for their families. Others explain that shame, stigma or fear of disease keep them from asking for help,” she said. “Some women limit their own movement for fear of infection. Others are kept at home by their families.” Dr. Noble stressed that isolation, quarantine and contact tracing are absolutely critical to halting the spread of Ebola, « but what these findings are telling us is that families are under enormous pressure because of Ebola, and women and girls are bearing much of the cost. » He underlined the need to keep services for women and girls open, accessible and funded, and to establish new ones where Ebola is spreading. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 25, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Bundibugyo Outbreak Shows Limits of Single-Pathogen Preparedness in DR Congo by November 24, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Bundibugyo Outbreak Shows Limits of Single-Pathogen Preparedness in DR Congo Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram The Democratic Republic of the Congo has served as an important setting for Ebola innovation, yet the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak demonstrates that key response capabilities remain closely linked to individual pathogens. Writing in Tropical Medicine and Health, Justin Kambale Kahingi and colleagues note that earlier advances substantially strengthened preparedness for Zaire ebolavirus through ring vaccination with recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus-based Ebola vaccine and the integration of clinical research into emergency response. However, those targeted capabilities reveal clear limits when confronting different outbreak threats. A major challenge highlighted in the report is that Bundibugyo virus lacks a licensed vaccine specifically indicated for prevention. While ring vaccination using recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus-based vaccine supported earlier interventions against Zaire ebolavirus, existing evidence remains insufficient to establish clinically meaningful protection from Ervebo against Bundibugyo virus disease in humans. Consequently, biomedical tools developed specifically for Zaire ebolavirus cannot be assumed to confer established clinical benefits during an outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus. Operational difficulties documented during the response in Bas-Uélé province further indicate that biomedical tools alone cannot ensure effective outbreak control. Response teams faced multiple practical constraints, including a temporary Ervebo stock-out, absent vaccination microplans, and limited mobility for vaccination teams. news.content_title: Ebola Outbreak Climbs to 11,645 Cases as Deaths Near 5700
news.content: The Ebola outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has reached 11,645 total confirmed cases and 5683 confirmed deaths as of November 17, 2026, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).1 The totals represent an increase of 500 cases (4.5%) and 246 deaths from the 11,145 cases and 5437 deaths reported as of November 10. DRC alone accounts for 11,613 cases and 5678 deaths.1,2 No cases tied to this outbreak have been reported in the US, and CDC considers the overall risk to the American public and travelers low.1 The outbreak remains the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record and is spreading substantially faster than previous Ebola outbreaks, according to the agency.1 How Fast Is the DRC Ebola Outbreak Growing? Confirmed deaths account for about 49% of confirmed cases. The outbreak surpassed 1000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation, compared with approximately 235 days for the 2018 DRC outbreak to pass the same mark. This is the 17th Ebola outbreak in DRC.1 CDC lists confirmed cases in the DRC provinces of Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu (North Kivu), Sud-Kivu (South Kivu), Sud-Ubangi (South Ubangi), Nord-Ubangi (North Ubangi), and Tshopo, though South Kivu has reported no confirmed cases since May 29.1 Suspected cases and deaths in DRC remain temporarily excluded from official counts pending data standardization, so totals are expected to change.1 Ebola Cases Reported Outside DRC Kenya's Ministry of Health has confirmed 9 cases and 2 deaths, all in Nairobi, with no reported community spread.1 The first Kenyan case, reported October 6, involved a man who traveled from DRC through Uganda to Nairobi, where he died in an isolation unit. Nigeria has reported 1 confirmed case, its first in the 2026 outbreak.1 Uganda has reported 20 confirmed cases, 2 confirmed deaths, 1 probable case, and 1 probable death, and its last confirmed patient was released from care July 16.
